papers.title: Comment on egusphere-2026-3653
papers.summary: Abstract. La Réunion is one of the French territories most exposed to natural risks. The island is exposed to seven major natural hazards: cyclones, floods, swells and tsunamis, landslides, earthquakes, wildfires, and volcanic eruptions. Numerous natural disasters have occurred on the island, as well as less significant natural events. This study presents a historical review of the direct impacts of natural events documented in departmental and national archives since human settlement on the island. Thus, in total 2,823 sources, referencing 1,266 events from 1655 to 2025 have been processed. The source's reliability is analyzed using a decision tree method. Based on the impacts, significance scores for each referenced event is established. An analysis of the evolution of impacts and mortality over time is conducted. A detailed geodatabase (HistoRiskRun) is created to capitalize information about natural hazards in La Réunion since its colonization. This database enhances documentation and understanding of past events and the evolution of risk management over time. This work provides elements to discuss the temporal evolution of impacts and mortalities associated with natural hazards and to relate these dynamics to the island’s geo-socio-historical context.

papers.title: Evolution of slope seepage field and stability assessment under rainfall conditions
papers.summary: To reveal the mechanism of the sliding instability in slopes under the coupling effect of rainfall intensity, duration, groundwater level, and geological structure, a bedding cutting slope of strongly weathered soil-rock mixture in southern China was tanken as the research object. Engineering geological survey was conducted to analyze the landslide. Based on saturated-unsaturated seepage theory, a finite element model under infiltration conditions was established to simulate the spatiotemporal evolution of pore water pressure, volumetric water content, and stability under the influences of various factors. The results show that heavy rainfall rapidly weakens shallow matric suction and raises pore water pressure and water content, resulting in a significant decrease in stability within a short time. Extension of duration leads to the advance of wetting front and the decrease of stability. High groundwater level superimposed heavy rainfall or long duration presents the most unfavorable stability.

papers.title: Spatial Distribution and Factors Influencing Clustered Landslides Triggered by Typhoon Rainstorms in Western Guangdong
papers.summary: In the context of global climate change, clustered shallow landslides triggered by extreme rainfall from typhoons have become among the most destructive geological disasters in the mountainous regions along the southeastern coast of China. However, a systematic understanding of the spatial clustering patterns of landslides and multifactorial nonlinear disaster mechanisms under complex topographic and geological conditions is lacking. This study focuses on clustered shallow landslides induced by Typhoon Sanba in the mountainous regions of western Guangdong in 2023. On the basis of high-resolution remote sensing imagery from Planet, a detailed landslide inventory is compiled. Combined with the use of an explainable machine learning framework, this study reveals the spatial distribution characteristics of landslides and multifactor synergistic driving mechanisms. The results indicate that the clustered landslides caused by Typhoon Sanba exhibit significant spatial clustering, with landslides concentrated primarily in areas containing weathered granite in low- to mid-elevation mountains affected by heavy rainfall, as well as in regions characterized by thick colluvial deposits and steep slopes. Rainfall is the primary factor that controls landslide development and exerts a distinct nonlinear threshold effect. Slope, thickness, and lithology amplify spatial variations in landslide development by jointly regulating the slope material structure and stability. Synergistic enhancement is observed between extreme rainfall and conditions such as weathered granite, thick colluvial deposits, and steep slopes, indicating that typhoon-induced clustered shallow landslides result from the combined coupling of extreme hydrological conditions and the regional topographic and geological environment. These findings provide a scientific basis for assessing typhoon and torrential rain disaster risks and for ensuring disaster prevention and mitigation in this region.

papers.title: An Interpretable Stacking Ensemble Framework for Defining Rainfall–Geoenvironmental Coupling Thresholds of Shallow Landslides
papers.summary: Rainfall-induced landslides exhibit marked spatio-temporal heterogeneity and multi-factor coupling. Existing susceptibility methods struggle to balance predictive accuracy with interpretability in nonlinear settings. This study addresses this gap by developing a Stacking ensemble framework integrated with SHAP analysis, using the July 2019 extreme rainfall-triggered landslides in northern Fujian and eastern Jiangxi as a case study. The framework builds an indicator system from multi-source data (topographic, geological, hydrological, and rainfall factors), screens key factors via correlation analysis, and constructs a Stacking model with Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM as base learners and Ridge Regression as the meta-learner. The Stacking model outperforms individual models on the test set (AUC = 0.8935, F1 = 0.800) and captures 90.9% of known landslide points within high and very high susceptibility zones. SHAP-based interpretability identifies rainfall as the dominant control, with soil thickness, slope gradient, and lithology as secondary factors. Each factor exhibits nonlinear marginal effects and condition-dependent behavior, with significant rainfall–terrain and rainfall–geotechnical interactions. The proposed framework not only improves prediction stability but also provides critical interpretability and decision-making support for landslide risk identification under extreme rainfall conditions.

papers.title: Dynamic Shear Band Propagation and Catastrophic Failure Criteria for Submarine Slopes Subjected to Progressive Externally Imposed Softening
papers.source: Journal of Marine Science and Engineering
papers.summary: Submarine landslides are a major geohazard in deep water, posing a severe threat to the safety of seabed infrastructure. Progressive failure on gentle slopes is commonly governed by strain softening of soils and shear band propagation (SBP). Several criteria have been developed analytically and numerically to predict catastrophic failure initiated from a pre-existing fully softened zone. In this study, dynamic SBPs during the progressive formation of an externally softened zone are investigated. Strength degradation is caused by both externally imposed softening and cumulative shear deformation. The governing dynamic equation is solved using a finite difference method. Depending on the extent of externally imposed softening, finite SBP followed by slope re-equilibration and catastrophic SBP are identified. The critical length of the externally softened zone required for catastrophic failure is quantified for different terminal strengths and formation durations. Two limiting lengths of the externally softened zone are determined. Below the lower limit, catastrophic failure cannot be triggered even when the zone is fully softened. Above the upper limit, only a slight strength reduction below the gravitational shear stress is sufficient to initiate catastrophic failure. The effect of the duration of externally imposed softening is also explored. Simple empirical criteria are proposed to predict both limiting lengths for practical application.

papers.title: Efforts to Increase Community Participation in Agroforestry Land Conservation on the Slopes of Mount Muria
papers.source: Journal of Business Social and Technology
papers.summary: Background: The slopes of Mount Muria serve as a water catchment area, a habitat for biodiversity, and a source of community livelihoods through agroforestry. However, land-use conversion, non-conservation-oriented cultivation practices, erosion, and landslides threaten the sustainability of these areas. Objective: This study aims to describe community activities on agroforestry land, identify the forms and assess the levels of community participation, and formulate strategies to strengthen participation in agroforestry land conservation in Colo Village, Dawe Subdistrict, Kudus Regency. Methods: A descriptive quantitative approach with a cross-sectional survey design was employed. From a population of 454 coffee farmers, 46 respondents were selected through proportional random sampling. Data were collected using questionnaires, observations, interviews, and documentation and were analyzed using descriptive percentages based on Abu Huraerah’s forms of participation and Arnstein’s Ladder of Citizen Participation. Results: Community participation was classified as good, with a score of 78.57%. Material contributions (85.76%) and labor contributions (81.30%) were dominant, while skills contributions (74.13%) required further strengthening. The level of participation was also categorized as good, with an overall score of 70.96%, comprising Nonparticipation (77.81%), Citizen Power (71.06%), and Tokenism (66.30%). Among the indicators, Information received the lowest score (60.51%). These findings demonstrate that conservation outcomes depend on the quality of community involvement throughout the land-management process. Conclusion: The study supports a community-empowerment-based conservation education approach and recommends strengthening farmer-group institutions, participatory extension services, technical skills, and information transparency to improve community participation in agroforestry land conservation.

papers.title: Initiation mechanism of irrigation-induced retrogressive loess landslides on the South Jingyang Tableland, China
papers.summary: Abstract Repeated sliding disturbs the slope structure and degrades soil mechanical properties, promoting the progressive development of retrogressive loess landslides on the South Jingyang Plateau, China. These landslides progressively encroach upon the plateau surface and have caused substantial casualties and property losses. Field investigations revealed that two subsequent retrogressive failures caused the landslide crown to retreat by approximately 8 and 7 m, respectively, suggesting that the near-crown zone formed after the initial failure underwent sustained disturbance and structural readjustment. Accordingly, undisturbed loess samples were collected from a sliding-disturbed zone approximately 5 m from the current crown (No.1) and a relatively undisturbed zone approximately 50 m from the crown (No.2). Consolidated undrained triaxial tests, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) infiltration tests, and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) analyses were conducted to systematically compare the strength, water-migration characteristics, and microstructural damage of the soils from the two zones, thereby elucidating the triggering mechanism of retrogressive landslides. The results indicate that: (1) The soil in the sliding-disturbed zone exhibited pronounced mechanical weakening. Under natural conditions, the average shear strength of No. 1 was approximately 20% lower than that of No. 2; under saturated conditions, its shear strength was only 71.9–90.0% of that in the relatively undisturbed zone. The disturbed soil was characterized by a higher proportion of large pores, weaker interparticle bonding, and more irregular pore geometries, making its mechanical behavior more sensitive to variations in water content. (2) The sliding-disturbed zone exhibited more pronounced water migration. The average signal intensity of the second peak in the NMR T₂ spectrum was approximately 1.97 times that of the relatively undisturbed zone, indicating a stronger water-filling response wi

papers.title: Fermium Hazard Mapper v3.0
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: An open Python pipeline and web application that trains flood susceptibility models on flood extents mapped from Sentinel-1 radar, scores every model on whole areas held out from training, and publishes asset-level and administrative-level flood and landslide risk for Bangladesh. Version 3.0 runs a national partition of eight flood regions over all 61 lowland districts plus the Chittagong Hill Tracts landslide region, and serves it through a FastAPI and MapLibre web application at https://fermium.systems/hazmapper.

papers.title: Storm Kristin (2026): Cascading Multi-Hazard Impacts of Sequential Events, Systemic Disruption and Governance Challenges in Mainland Portugal
papers.summary: Storm Kristin, which struck Portugal on 28 January 2026, generated one of the most disruptive multi-hazard events in recent decades. Extreme winds, followed by successive episodes of intense rainfall, triggered a cascade of impacts across central-western Portugal and parts of Spain, including flooding, coastal erosion, hazardous nearshore currents, and numerous landslides. Approximately eight million pine trees were blown down, obstructing transport networks and damaging power and telecommunications infrastructures. Widespread interruptions to essential services, industrial activity, and daily life persisted for more than two months. Although fatalities were limited due to the timing of the strongest winds, the event caused extensive damage to residential and industrial buildings, large-scale population displacement, and significant economic losses. In response, the Portuguese Government declared a state of calamity, affecting around 17.1% of the national population. This paper examines the cascading interactions among hazards and their systemic consequences, highlighting critical shortcomings in scientific knowledge, risk governance, and societal preparedness. It also discusses the prolonged recovery challenges, including the heightened wildfire risk posed by vast accumulations of fallen wood. Finally, the paper proposes an integrated assessment framework based on a dynamic “Disruption Index” and presents recommendations to support recovery and strengthen resilience to future compound and cascading disasters.

papers.title: Deterministic design optimization for soil nail walls in a Brazilian highway construction
papers.summary: Soil nail walls are widely used for slope stabilization in transportation infrastructure; however, their design still relies predominantly on manual, trial-and-error procedures or simplified Limit Equilibrium Method (LEM) analyses, which do not ensure optimality. Existing optimization studies are typically limited to idealized problems, lack integration with industry-standard Finite Element Method (FEM) tools, and rarely incorporate realistic construction stages or current design codes. This study addresses these limitations by proposing a fully automated Deterministic Design Optimization (DDO) framework that integrates the Sequential Least Squares Programming (SLSQP) algorithm with the commercial FEM software Plaxis 2D via Python scripting. The choice of Plaxis 2D enables rigorous simulation of soil–structure interaction, staged construction, and advanced constitutive behavior, while the scripting interface allows seamless automation, iterative model updating, and efficient exploration of the design space. The framework is applied to a real Brazilian highway case study, incorporating the requirements of the national standard ABNT NBR 16920-2. Optimization variables include nail length, face inclination, and total construction cost. Results demonstrate robust convergence and highlight the critical role of cost-based objective functions in achieving economically efficient designs. Validation against LEM analyses performed in Slide2 shows good agreement in factors of safety, with differences observed in predicted failure mechanisms. The proposed approach provides a practical, code-compliant, and scalable framework for automated geotechnical design, with significant potential for cost reduction in large infrastructure projects.

papers.title: Right on time: evaluating accuracy and timing of burn-severity assessments to support post-fire management
papers.summary: Abstract Effective wildfire impact assessment and post-fire management rely on burn-severity maps that accurately characterize fire effects on vegetation and soils. These maps inform time-sensitive activities such as post-fire flood and debris-flow modeling, risk mitigation for homes and communities, and ecosystem recovery planning, but the satellite observations used to generate them are often obstructed or delayed by smoke, clouds, and snow. Across 9,129 large fires (≥ 404 ha) in Canada and the United States from 2016–2024, we quantified post-fire data obstruction and evaluated observational latency – defined as the time required to acquire the first usable scene – for four freely available moderate-resolution remote sensing datasets: Landsat, Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2, and the Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 (HLS) product. For multispectral datasets (Landsat, Sentinel-2, and HLS), cloud cover was the primary source of data obstruction, particularly in mesic and coastal regions, whereas Sentinel-1 (synthetic aperture radar) can penetrate clouds. Consequently, Sentinel-1 had the shortest observational latency (median = 4 days), followed by HLS (7 days), Sentinel-2 (10 days), and Landsat (17 days). Likewise, one-month composite imagery from Sentinel-1 (89.6%) and HLS (82.8%) achieved near-complete coverage for most fires, substantially better than Sentinel-2 (70.5%) and Landsat (56.1%). Despite its widespread use in operational burn-severity mapping, Landsat provided the slowest and least complete early post-fire coverage. For 77 fires in forested ecosystems, we also evaluated relationships between early post-fire imagery and field-derived burn-severity measurements collected 0–3 years after fire. All multispectral datasets corresponded well with field data and reliably identified areas of near-total canopy loss using imagery acquired within two months after fire (> 80% balanced accuracy), performing nearly as well as extended assessments using imagery from a full post-f

papers.title: Peak ground acceleration underestimates narrow-band seismic amplification on mountain slopes
papers.summary: Abstract Topographic amplification is widely invoked to explain strong shaking and slope failure in mountainous terrain, yet direct field observations remain limited. Here we analyze 24 regional earthquakes recorded by a four-station strong-motion array spanning a ridge crest, a valley bottom, and two contrasting slope facets on a single ridge in central Japan. Peak ground acceleration (PGA) and frequency-dependent measures reveal markedly different representations of local seismic response. PGA ratios vary among events and are positively associated with epicentral distance; however, earthquake magnitude also increases with distance, so source-size and propagation-distance effects cannot be separated in this catalog. In contrast, the NS slope exhibits a persistent narrow-band station-to-valley Fourier spectral-ratio peak at 3.5–4.0 Hz that remains stable across events and processing choices. Absolute spectra confirm enhanced energy at the slope in this band, while also showing that a relative spectral depression at the valley reference contributes to the large ratio magnitude. Most importantly, the geometric-mean 5%-damped response-spectral ratio reaches 6.67 at 0.277 s (3.61 Hz), compared with a corresponding full-record geometric-mean horizontal PGA ratio of 1.13. These observations show that PGA can substantially under-represent frequency-specific elastic response on mountain slopes, while the responsible mechanism cannot be uniquely attributed to topography or near-surface structure alone.

papers.title: Deep Learning Paper
papers.summary: This dataset contains the geospatial and landslide-related data used in the study “comparative assessment of ML and DL models.” The dataset was prepared for developing and evaluating landslide susceptibility models using machine learning and deep learning approaches.

papers.title: Effect of air permeability at the bottom on rainfall infiltration
papers.summary: In geotechnical engineering, the permeability of air through soil has been recognized as a factor influencing the dynamics of subsurface water pressure, thereby playing a role in determining the stress levels experienced by the soil. This study employed the finite element method to evaluate the rainfall infiltration process, taking into account various air permeability boundary conditions, including air ventilation, air sealing, and quantified air permeability. The research also explored the relationship between boundary air permeability and infiltration capability, pore pressure, and saturation distribution. Two comparative analyses under ventilation and air sealing conditions were conducted using GeoStudio software to verify the validity of the numerical calculations, and errors consistently remained below 30%. The artificial rainfall simulation tests and automatic data acquisition were conducted under two distinct conditions: ventilation and air sealing. The results showed that a decrease in boundary air permeability had a pronounced effect on infiltration. The relationship between boundary air permeability and infiltration capability exhibited a logarithmic pattern. Moreover, lower boundary permeability values were directly correlated with increased pore air pressure during the rainfall infiltration process, resulting in a decelerated advancement of the wetting front. When comparing the test data under ventilation and air-sealing conditions, it was observed that air sealing restricted air escape, hindering rainwater infiltration and significantly reducing the infiltration rate. This also led to a gradual transformation of the saturated zone within the slope.

papers.title: Geotechnical Engineering Explained: Soil, Foundations & Earth System Design
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Geotechnical Engineering Explained: Soil, Foundations & Earth System Design is an open educational resource (OER) curriculum module establishing the continuum mechanics, subsurface testing protocols, and computational modeling paradigms governing earth-structure interactions. The module establishes a rigorous geotechnical engineering foundation across nine specialized domains: Subsurface Mechanics & Testing: Soil mechanics (Mohr-Coulomb shear criteria, Terzaghi 1D consolidation theory, Darcy's seepage law), rock mass characterization (RMR/GSI), in-situ exploration (SPT, CPTu piezocone, pressuremeter, borehole coring), and laboratory testing (triaxial compression, oedometer, Atterberg plasticity limits). Foundation & Earth Retention Systems: Shallow spread/raft foundation bearing capacity, deep bored shafts and driven pile friction mechanics, retaining wall lateral earth pressures (Rankine/Coulomb), and deep excavation shoring. Geotechnical Hazards & Ground Improvement: Limit equilibrium and finite element slope stability (infinite slope equilibrium, Bishop method of slices), seismic liquefaction triggers, deep soil mixing, dynamic compaction, vibro-replacement stone columns, and bio-mediated cementation (MICP). Key Analytical & Technical Features: Foundation System & Ground Modification Trade-off Matrix: Multi-variable comparison evaluating Shallow Spread Footings, Driven Precast Concrete Piles, Bored Cast-in-Situ Shafts, and Vibro-Stone Columns across load capacities, stratigraphy limits, vibration noise, and lifecycle risk allocation. Worked Numerical Engineering Application: Multi-step Terzaghi bearing capacity derivation for continuous strip footings under general shear failure, calculating surcharge overburden contributions, ultimate capacity, allowable capacity (FS = 3.0), and permissible wall line loads. Interactive Slope Stability & Landslide Simulator: Client-side dynamic canvas tool evaluating infinite hillside equilibrium, displaying pore water ratio degr

papers.title: An integrated modeling method for rainfall-induced geohazard chains: coupling landslide mobilization and flow-state transition
papers.summary: Extreme rainfall in mountain catchments can trigger shallow landslides, debris flows, and sediment-laden floods as interconnected geohazard chains. This study proposes a coupling-oriented modeling framework that links rainfall-induced landslide-source mobilization with downstream flow-state transition. Rather than introducing separate submodels, the main methodological contribution is to convert hydrologically activated slope instability into time-, geometry-, and volume-explicit sediment supply and to route this supply as a single evolving solid–water mixture for identifying slide-like, debris-flow-like, and flood-dominated pathways. The method was applied to the 2023 extreme rainfall event in Beijing, China. Hydrological benchmarking showed that the dynamic front–perched layer formulation better captured localized pressure-head development near landslide-prone locations than bucket-type storage and Green–Ampt infiltration. The cellular-automaton (CA)-based source module generated rainfall-aligned shallow landslide release areas with explicit timing, depth, and object-scale morphology. Downstream simulation showed that released material mainly formed short-lived, high-concentration pulses rather than a sustained debris-flow-dominated process. During the main rainfall stage, released landslide volume was approximately 3.29 × 10 4 m 3 , whereas additional scour contributed only approximately 7%. The event therefore followed a rapid-dilution pathway toward flood-dominated, sediment-laden transport.

papers.title: Assessment of Safety and Hazard Management Practices and Emergency Preparedness among Employees in Hospitals of Nepal
papers.summary: Background: Hospitals in Nepal operate in the environment that is vulnerable to biological, chemical, physical, ergonomic, psychosocial, fire, and disaster risks. Being prone to earthquakes, floods, landslides, fires and disease outbreaks, Nepal needs hospital-based employee safety and disaster preparedness programs. Objectives: This paper will present evidence on occupational and environmental risks, practices of safety and hazard management, disaster preparedness, organizational issues and knowledge gaps of selected hospitals in Nepal. Methods: This is a narrative review based on research articles specific to Nepal, disaster preparedness literature, and selected guidelines on occupational safety, infection prevention and control, biomedical waste, and hospital disaster preparedness. Evidence is provided thematically. Results: Evidence reveals a number of risks and issues related to occupational and environmental safety, including needlesticks, infection prevention and control, personal protective equipment, biomedical waste, psychosocial issues, and preparedness for emergencies. While 84% of 25 hub hospitals have disaster plans, only 33% of hospitals with disaster plans had fire safety measures. Assessment of three public hospitals through Hospital Safety Index placed them in category B, which means that they have moderate safety and preparedness. Conclusion: Hospital safety requires implementation, not policies. Regular training, simulation exercises, hazard assessments, availability of resources, communication, incident command systems, occupational health services, and monitoring are critical for preparedness and resilience. Novelty: This paper brings together the topics of occupational safety, infection prevention, environmental health, disaster preparedness, and hospital resilience in the same Nepalese context.

papers.title: Stability Assessment of a Large-Scale Landslide in the Minjiang River Basin Based on UAV Oblique Photogrammetry and Numerical Simulation
papers.summary: The West Route of the South-to-North Water Diversion Project traverses geologically fragile alpine terrain where large pre-existing landslides pose long-term risks to infrastructure safety and sustainable corridor development. Taking the Xianiba landslide in the upper Minjiang River Basin (plan area approximately 8.6 × 104 m2) as a case study, this study integrates unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) oblique photogrammetry, three-dimensional geological modeling, and FLAC3D numerical analysis to investigate the relationship between short-term rainfall infiltration and deep-seated hydraulic reactivation. Under natural conditions, the three-dimensional model reaches mechanical equilibrium, and the strength-reduction method (SRM) gives a factor of safety (Fs) of 1.656, while the rear and upper portions of the sliding interface show stronger localized shear response. A separate one-dimensional infiltration analysis was used to constrain the depth of direct short-term matrix wetting, showing that the 24 h rainfall-affected depth increases from approximately 0.43 m at 20 mm/d to 1.00 m at 150 mm/d. Prescribed hydraulic-head scenarios were then used to quantify the stability evolution of the deep sliding interface. Across the re-equilibrated prescribed-head cases (h = 1.0–2.25 m), Fs remains close to 1.64, whereas interface shear displacement and current shear-yield response increase markedly with hydraulic head. The model can re-establish equilibrium under a hydraulic head of 2.25 m but develops sustained sliding at 2.5 m and above, defining a model-conditioned transition range of approximately 2.25–2.50 m. These results indicate that short-term rainfall mainly controls shallow wetting, whereas potential reactivation of the deep-seated landslide is more strongly associated with hydraulic weakening along the pre-existing sliding interface. The 24 h rainfall cases are therefore interpreted as short-term matrix-infiltration scenarios rather than complete field-scale recharge pathwa

papers.title: Implementing a climate-resilient and inclusive WASH guidance in Indonesia: A mixed-methods case study
papers.summary: Climate change increasingly disrupts water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) services, disproportionately affecting women, children, people with disabilities, and groups with limited adaptive resources. Evidence remains limited on how WASH programs integrate climate resilience, equity, and social inclusion and on the conditions that enable benefits to reach households. Researchers examined how Climate Change Response for Inclusive WASH (CCRIW) guidance was implemented and adapted within routine programming in Indonesia, how implementation outcomes related to post-implementation household access, and which contextual factors enabled or constrained such access. Researchers conducted a mixed-methods study using program data collected between August 2023 and October 2024. Data included key informant interviews (n = 29) and a group discussion (n = 10). Quantitative data included village workshop records (n = 91) and household surveys and observations (n = 1,243) from 12 villages affected by floods, landslides, and drought. Researchers used descriptive statistics and logistic regression and triangulated the findings with deductive qualitative analysis informed by an implementation science framework. Results indicated that CCRIW guidance was perceived as relevant but was adapted during implementation rather than adopted as a complete stand-alone protocol. These adaptations appeared to improve short-term practicality while reducing consistent application, depth of learning, and recall of CCRIW as a distinct approach. Communities primarily adopted lower-cost actions aligned with immediate needs, available resources, and perceived feasibility. Household modifications supported more resilient and inclusive access but could not replace system-level investments under severe hazards. Regression models showed district-level associations for several facility-specific outcomes, limited associations with multiple-hazard exposure, and no consistent associations with reported household c

papers.title: Effects of buffer-zone sampling on random forest landslide susceptibility assessment
papers.summary: The selection of negative samples is critical to landslide susceptibility assessment, yet the effect of their spatial distance from landslide locations remains insufficiently understood. This study investigated how buffer-zone sampling ranges affect the generalisation performance of random forest models in Lin’an District, Hangzhou, China. Using a 1:1 ratio of positive to negative samples, six datasets were constructed with negative samples randomly selected within buffer ranges of 0.5–1.5 to 0.5–6 km. Nine conditioning factors were used for model development, and SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) analysis was employed for model interpretation. Results showed a clear scale-dependent effect of buffer distance. Model performance improved with increasing sampling range up to an optimal limit, with the 0.5–5 km buffer achieving the highest predictive accuracy and most reliable susceptibility zonation. Further expansion to 0.5–6 km reduced model performance. SHAP analysis indicated that sampling scale altered the statistical representation of negative samples, thereby affecting feature importance and model responses. These findings demonstrate that buffer distance should be evaluated as a sampling-scale parameter rather than selected solely by empirical convention, providing a practical basis for optimising negative-sample selection in regional landslide susceptibility modelling.

papers.title: Beyond Abandonment: Mapping Italy’s Ghost Towns Between Heritage, Marginality and Risks Toward Revitalization
papers.summary: The article presents the results of a national inventory of abandoned settlements—ghost towns—in Italy while also exploring possible strategies for revitalising these unique sites. The time window considered spans from the 18th to the 21st centuries. A tailored methodology, divided into six main phases, involved an in-depth bibliographical analysis and the compilation of a preliminary list of abandoned settlements. Transparent inclusion and exclusion criteria were then defined, followed by the selection and updating of the list of sites through different sources of information. Finally, a geodatabase was developed with a set of information fields for the standardised inventory and cataloguing of ghost towns that can also be applied in other national contexts. We identified 702 ghost towns divided into three typological categories, distributed unevenly across the country, with a cluster in the north-west of the peninsula. The abandoned settlements are primarily located in hilly and mountainous areas, with abandonment chiefly caused by anthropogenic drivers, particularly emigration, while natural causes, mainly earthquakes and landslides, are also significant. The total abandoned area amounts to 7.8 km2, approximately equivalent to the size of Venice’s historic centre. Chronologically, the phenomenon is most concentrated in the post-World War II period and the following decades. The comparison between the geographical distribution of ghost towns and the national classification of inner areas suggests that the current classification can be partially read as the contemporary outcome of historical trajectories of marginalisation and depopulation of those territories. Therefore, the dataset can provide useful insights for the national strategy for inner areas. Furthermore, the geodatabase makes it possible to identify future revitalisation strategies with special attention to tourism. This innovative research therefore offers, for the first time, a framework useful not on

papers.title: Slope Stability and Reinforcement Analysis Using Front Cantol Cantilever Ground-Type Retaining Wall
papers.summary: Soil, as a key material in geotechnical construction, has important mechanical parameters such as cohesion (c), internal friction angle (φ), and unit weight (γ), which are significantly affected by hydrological conditions. Rainwater infiltration can increase pore pressure and reduce soil shear strength, potentially triggering landslides, especially on steep slopes. The 2025 landslide in Aek Godang Arbaan Village, Onang Ganjang District, Humbang Hasundutan Regency, highlighted the vulnerability of the high slopes of provincial roads, which play a strategic role in regional connectivity. This study calculates the slope Safety Factor (SF) using the direct shear test shear strength parameters and the soil unit weight. The findings of the study provide a basis for designing an effective retaining wall to improve slope stability and support efforts to mitigate landslide risk to road infrastructure in the research area. Evaluation using the Fellenius and Bishop methods indicates that the slope was in critical condition. The geometric parameters of a slope, especially its height and slope angle, are the dominant factors that increase the likelihood of landslides. Laboratory test results indicate that the local soil exhibits index parameters and engineering properties that are sensitive to changes in moisture content. The relatively high plasticity and the influence of rainwater infiltration reduce cohesion and the internal friction angle, thereby reducing bearing capacity and slope stability. Furthermore, the analysis indicates that the alternative reinforcement using cantilever retaining walls is the most appropriate for the geotechnical and geological conditions of the research site. The implementation of this design significantly improves the slope's SF and maintains the function of provincial roads as strategic transportation infrastructure.

papers.title: Intelligent Computational Systems for Scientific Problems: Principles, Methodologies, and Intricate Data Classification
papers.source: The American Journal of Applied Sciences
papers.summary: The increasing complexity, dimensionality, and dynamical nature of scientific and engineering problems have created a growing demand for computational systems capable of learning from data, representing nonlinear relationships, solving optimization problems, and supporting decision-making under uncertainty. Intelligent computational systems integrate concepts from machine learning, neural computation, optimization, distributed computing, signal processing, control theory, and scientific computing to address problems that are difficult to solve through conventional analytical techniques alone. This review examines the theoretical foundations, methodological development, and application-oriented characteristics of such systems, with particular emphasis on neural architectures, deep learning, recurrent computation, intelligent optimization, adaptive control, distributed computation, and data classification. The analysis synthesizes the supplied literature to establish a coherent framework connecting foundational learning models with contemporary scientific and engineering applications. The reviewed literature demonstrates that intelligent computation has evolved from relatively compact neural models toward multilayer, recurrent, distributed, and hybrid computational architectures. Early developments in deep learning established mechanisms for learning hierarchical representations, while recurrent and complex-valued neural models expanded computational learning toward temporal, dynamic, and mathematically structured problems (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997; Hinton et al., 2006; Bengio, 2009; LeCun et al., 2015). Subsequent work has demonstrated that intelligent algorithms can also be integrated with optimization and control mechanisms to solve time-varying systems, robotic motion problems, portfolio-selection problems, engineering prediction tasks, and infrastructure-management problems. In parallel, cloud and volunteer distributed computing have demonstrated how comp

papers.title: Improvement of Soil Liquefaction by Micro-Pile and Soil Grouting for Liqiefaction-Induced Flowslide: A Numerical Assessment
papers.summary: Soil liquefaction is a major geotechnical hazard that can cause bearing capacity loss, lateral spreading, and flowslides, particularly in mildly sloping ground. Loose, saturated sands with shallow groundwater tables are highly vulnerable because seismic shaking induces contraction and generates excess pore water pressure (EPWP). Although several countermeasures have been proposed, systematic evaluations of micro-piles (MP) and soil grouting (GT) under mildly sloping liquefiable ground remain limited. This study addresses this gap through three-dimensional finite element simulations in OpenSeesPL using Chi-Chi earthquake loading. Design parameters considered include pile length, diameter, and spacing for MP, as well as grouting depth and improvement ratio for GT. The results show that both MP and GT effectively delay the buildup of EPWP. However, MP consistently provides better control of lateral deformation, whereas GT primarily reduces settlement but may increase inertia due to added unit weight. Sensitivity analyses highlight the critical influence of pile geometry and spacing in MP performance, and depth and improvement ratio in GT effectiveness. These findings indicate that MP is more suitable for sites prone to lateral spreading, while GT is advantageous for conditions requiring settlement control. The outcomes provide practical guidance for engineers in designing liquefaction mitigation strategies in earthquake-prone regions.

papers.title: The use of near-surface geophysics for monitoring slopes that affect transport infrastructure
papers.summary: Landslides on transportation networks are becoming increasingly prevalent in response to environmental change, at the same time as demand placed on road and rail infrastructure is growing in line with population growth and economic development. To minimise the impact of slope instability on vital transport infrastructure, as well as on terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems, public safety, communities, local heritage, and the economy, and to better inform decision making, there is a need for remote-condition-monitoring systems to reveal processes that are precursors to slope failure. Here, the application of a novel electrical resistivity tomography (ERT) system (Proactive infrastructure Monitoring and Evaluation (PRIME)) for monitoring unstable slopes that affect transport infrastructure is examined. The system provides near-real-time data collection via a telemetric link. 4-Dimensional resistivity models (3-D with a time-lapse element) are presented in the context of moisture content and soil suction, two parameters known to influence slope stability. Building upon relationships evident in the field, the development of laboratory-based petrophysical relationships that relate electrical resistivity to moisture content and soil suction directly is also discussed. 4-D ERT models were calibrated using these petrophysical relationships to provide insights into complex spatial and temporal variations in moisture content and soil suction. Two study areas are considered here, enabling different controls on electrical resistivity to be examined. The Ripley Landslide in the Thompson River Valley, British Columbia, Canada, threatens the serviceability of two national railway lines. Here, 4-D ERT models reveal complex hydrogeological pathways, providing new insights into the subsurface processes in an active, natural landslide. Freeze-thaw cycles also impact the subsurface resistivity here, which highlights the need to consider the impact of temperature when inferring changes in

papers.title: YeNCLD (Yenisei North cryogenic landslides Dataset): locations of ALDS and RTS in the Yenisei North (north-eastern part of West Siberia)
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Main Info A variety of cryogenic slope processes, including ALDS (active-layer detachment slides) and RTS (retrogressive thaw slumps), occur in the north of West Siberia. Previous research into these processes only partly cover the Yenisei North, and only in the context of identifying the RTS, but not ALDS. This region covers more than 60,000 km2, where we mapped ALDS and RTS locations using remote sensing imagery from 2000 to 2025. We identified the spatial patterns and determining factors that control the distribution of both types of cryogenic landslide along a latitudinal regiongradient spanning approximately 450 km from the Arctic tundra to the southern forest tundra. Yenisei North Cryogenic Landslides Dataset (YeNCLD) compiled in the study is available here. This data supplement to the article Kizyakov A.I., Streletskaya I.D., Wetterich S., Ermolov A.A., Derkacheva A.A., Kopyl E.A., Leibman M.O. Cryogenic landslides in the Yenisei North (north-eastern part of West Siberia) Data structure In addition to the compiled database of RTS and ALDS points, datasets of non-landslide points were created. For each cryogenic landslide type, datasets with filtering threshold distances of 500 m and 1000 m were created. Details are provided in the original article. Archive YeNCLD_v2.rar contains ArcGIS shapefiles with a) RTS, b) ALDS, c) non RTS, d) non ALDS locations. The structure of attribute tables for shapefiles is identical and includes the following fields: The structure of attribute tables for RTS and ALDS is identical and includes the following fields: aspect – surface exposition in degrees, slope – slope inclination, in degrees, range500 – vertical dissection of the terrain within 500 m grid, in m, ALT_mean – active layer thickness, averaged for 2001-2021, in m, T10m – mean annual ground temperature at 10 m depth, °C, geol_ind_n – main groups of Quaternary deposits, veget_zone – name of vegetation zone. papers.title: Synergising local geo-environmental characteristics with spatial context for enhancing landslide susceptibility mapping
papers.summary: Data-driven methods are widely used in landslide susceptibility mapping (LSM) because they can effectively model the complex relationships between landslides and geo-environmental conditions. Existing data-driven approaches generally follow two types of data representations. Pixel-based models focus solely on the geo-environmental characteristics of a specific landslide but neglect the influence of its surrounding environment. Patch-based models incorporate surrounding spatial context but may include pixels with weak or no spatial relevance to the target landslide location. To address this limitation, this study proposes a Local-Geo and Spatial Context Fusion (LGSCF) strategy, which synergises the geo-environmental characteristics of landslide points with their corresponding spatial context through a feature-wise modulation mechanism. We tested the LGSCF strategy by integrating it into several representative convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures, creating nine different LGSCF-based models. The primary study area covers approximately 2644 km² across Jenai and Sinyi Townships in Nantou County, Taiwan, and the dataset comprises 5332 landslide samples and an equal number of non-landslide samples. The results show that LGSCF-based models consistently outperform their corresponding baselines, achieving F1-scores up to 87.09% and AUC values up to 0.9472. Furthermore, the susceptibility maps produced by LGSCF-based models show that known landslides are more accurately concentrated in “very high” susceptibility zones with fewer misclassifications. These findings demonstrate that our fusion strategy can significantly improve the accuracy of landslide susceptibility mapping.

papers.title: BigLeak - Archaeology
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: BigLeak Archaeology BigLeak Archaeology V1.3 – A Formally Falsifiable Compression Protocol for Symbolic Systems This independent research document tests the hypothesis of a domain-general cognitive compression protocol underlying prehistoric symbolic clusters. We define a 5-slot essence E = {σ Origin, κ Relation, π Individuation, τ Time, γ Transition} and operationalize compliance through four explicit axioms: |E|=5, E⊂V, |V|≥13 (implements |V|/|E|≥2.5), and S(E)/S(V) ∈ [0.6;0.7]. Entropy calculations, codebook V1-V4 and a runnable Python evaluator are included for full reproducibility (Cohen K_IRR = 0.72). N=15 symbolic clusters from 18,000 BP to 1000 AD across four continents pass all axioms; a contrast sample of 4 complex structures passes 0/4, demonstrating discriminant validity. After quantitative taphonomic analysis (infinite-slope Factor of Safety FS=1.38-1.96 = marginally stable, ∼100% noise), the originally preregistered test case Göbekli Tepe Enclosure F is retained as control. Primary is now the landslide-resilient Ħal Saflieni Hypogeum, Malta (FS≈183.6, <1% noise, carved from in situ limestone bedrock), with Chauvet Cave and Yazılıkaya as secondary / tertiary. The framework is presented without cosmological binding and is fully specified for open scientific

papers.title: Initiation thresholds and statistical properties of rainfall-induced landslides under centennial-scale variations in land use and land cover and rainfall characteristics
AI-based procedure for extracting spatial and temporal information on rainfall-induced landslides from textual sources
papers.summary: Abstract Comprehensive landslide catalogues require accurate and reproducible spatial and temporal information, yet manual extraction from textual sources is time-consuming and affected by inter- and intra-operator variability. We present AIDE4LAND (Artificial Intelligence-based procedure for Data Extraction for LANDslides), a novel structured procedure that combines Large Language Models and prompt engineering to automatically extract temporal and spatial information on rainfall-induced landslides from textual sources. The procedure is organized as a two-step process: (i) temporal extraction, which reconstructs the date and time of occurrence according to explicit hierarchical rules and assigns standardized temporal accuracy levels, and (ii) spatial extraction, which progressively determines geographic coordinates through structured queries and reverse-geocoding validation using OpenStreetMap APIs via Anthropic’s Model Context Protocol. The workflow was developed through iterative prompt-refinement cycles, involving 2162 tests conducted on 725 textual sources (664 written in Italian and 61 in English) published between 2011 and 2025. Validation of AIDE4LAND outputs against a manually compiled expert dataset revealed a high level of agreement, with 87% of cases demonstrating maximum concordance in terms of temporal and spatial attribution. By combining standardized rules, explicit accuracy classification, and automated consistency checks, AIDE4LAND formalizes expert reasoning into transparent and reproducible procedural rules, thereby reducing interpretative variability and ensuring transparent and systematic traceability in the decision process. The procedure significantly accelerates catalogue updates and provides a transferable and reproducible methodological framework for constructing structured rainfall-induced landslide catalogues, supporting hazard assessment, rainfall-threshold definition, and early warning applications.

papers.title: Guangdong rainfall-induced landslide inventory and environmental variables for latent-regime analysis
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: This dataset contains the processed research data supporting the study “Latent infiltration regimes mediate environmental controls on delayed rainfall-induced landslides.” The dataset comprises 2,025 rainfall-related landslide records from Guangdong Province, South China, together with the environmental variables used to investigate delayed landslide responses to rainfall forcing. The dataset includes landslide identifiers and locations, occurrence and rainfall-event timing information, landslide lag time, soil thickness, slope, aspect, lithology, and antecedent cumulative rainfall over 3-h, 6-h, 12-h, 1-day, 2-day, and 3-day windows. Figure-level data and model-output files used to evaluate the analyses reported in the manuscript are also provided. The dataset supports the statistical analyses, Bayesian latent-regime inference, model selection, environmental attribution, and figure generation presented in the manuscript. A data dictionary describing the variables, units, and processing information is included in the archive. Original third-party source records subject to redistribution restrictions are not redistributed in this archive. Their provenance and access conditions are documented in the accompanying documentation.

papers.title: Forensic back-analysis of a reactivated deep-seated landslide in volcanic residual soils of the Cisumdawu highway KM 178, Indonesia
papers.summary: Abstract Background This study is a forensic back-analysis of the 2021 embankment failure at KM 178 of the Cisumdawu Highway, Indonesia. The post-failure investigation identified weak subsurface materials but no discrete failure horizon, and the mechanism was never established. Six independent lines of field evidence were assembled, from UAV LiDAR geomorphology to paired triaxial and direct shear testing. A two-dimensional Morgenstern–Price model was built with the failure surface fixed from that evidence while material parameters were calibrated. Pore pressure was represented as a material-specific ratio rather than a piezometric surface, the residual soil permeability being too low to transmit storm rainfall to depth. Uncertainty was propagated by Monte Carlo simulation. Results The alignment crosses a valley floored by relict landslide deposits, with arcuate paleo-scarps on the upper slope. The weathering profile grades from residual silty clay through residual silty sand to weathered tuff, placing a granular horizon within low-permeability clay, so permeability is not monotonic with depth. Inclinometers installed after the rupture intercepted a shear horizon at 559 and 536 m elevation, recording 15 cm and 10 cm of cumulative wet-season displacement, while the instrument monitored during the dry season recorded none. Deeper horizons remain active but could not be traced laterally, indicating a larger relict complex. That horizon coincides with N-SPT below 10 enclosed within material returning 20 to 30, a strength inversion weathering cannot produce, and with gravelly deposits of low resistivity. Without imposed pore pressure it is not the critical surface, returning 1.40 against 1.29 for a shallower surface within the embankment. It becomes critical only when the pore-pressure ratio reaches about 0.37, at an operational friction angle of 20.5°, below the measured peak of 29°. Peer Review Report For: Physical and Mechanical Characteristics of Soil as a Controlling Factor in Landslides in Curug Panjang Village, Cihuni Hamlet, Lebak, Banten: Analysis of Distribution, Normality, and Inter-parameter Relationships [version 2; peer review: 1 approved, 1 approved with reservations]
papers.summary: Background Landslide occurrence is strongly influenced by the physical and mechanical properties of subsurface soil; this study evaluates these properties in residual soil from Kampung Cihuni, Lebak Regency, as a controlling factor in landslides. Methods Thirty residual soil samples were collected at a depth of 0–1 m using a grid sampling method. Laboratory testing covered natural water content (w); specific gravity and unit weight, used to derive void ratio (e); the plasticity index (PI) from the Atterberg limits; and Unconsolidated Undrained (UU) triaxial testing for cohesion (c) and internal friction angle (φ). The distribution of each parameter was evaluated using histograms, Q-Q plots, and the Shapiro-Wilk normality test, while inter-parameter relationships were analysed using linear regression (R 2 ) and Spearman correlation (ρ). Results The Shapiro-Wilk test showed that cohesion (c) and void ratio (e) are normally distributed, whereas water content (w), PI, and friction angle (φ) are not. PI values for the plastic samples (n = 26) ranged from 13.8% to 86.7%, and φ ranged from 5.48° to 20.5°; the relationship between the two was weakly positive (R 2 = 0.151, p = 0.050; Spearman ρ = 0.244, p = 0.229). Cohesion ranged from 4.41–52.47 kPa but showed a very weak, non-significant relationship with water content (R 2 = 0.028, p = 0.376), as did void ratio with φ (R 2 = 0.089, p = 0.110). Conclusions Relationships among the physical and mechanical parameters were weak and mostly non-significant, so the reduction in soil shear strength cannot be explained by any single parameter alone. Because the UU triaxial test represents total-stress conditions, it cannot directly explain rainfall infiltration and pore-water pressure change as a landslide trigger, though it offers an initial picture of the residual soil’s engineering characteristics as a controlling factor in the area’s landslide susceptibility.

papers.title: Permafrost Monitoring in the Central Alaska Network of National Parks
papers.summary: The three national park units which comprise the National Park Service Inventory and Monitoring Program’s Central Alaska Network (CAKN: Wrangell-St. Elias, Denali, and Yukon-Charley Rivers) are underlain by permafrost—ground that remains at or below 0°C for at least two, but typically many, years. Much of that permafrost, however, is geographically discontinuous, thin, and close to the melting point of water. Under the warming conditions that characterize these parks, permafrost thaw is likely to have significant impacts on the landscapes of these parks. These impacts may include development of thermokarst, landslides and slumping, changes in hydrology and vegetation, growth and/or drainage of lakes, enhanced release of greenhouse gases, and decay of characteristic permafrost features like pingos and rock glaciers. The CAKN permafrost monitoring program is designed to monitor a subset of these changes over multiple decades, and focuses on tracking changes in the thermal and physical state of permafrost. Collected data will contribute directly to the Global Terrestrial Network for Permafrost, the primary international permafrost monitoring program. Thermal changes will be monitored with a broad network of shallow (<3 m) soil temperature measurements, and also with temperature measurements from a single deep (29-70 m) borehole adjacent to each park. These measurements will mostly be conducted in collaboration with existing monitoring programs to leverage existing resources. Physical changes will be monitored with a network of active layer thickness measurements that use late-summer mechanical probing to determine maximum thaw depth on fine-grained permafrost soils. The thaw depth measurements will be co-located with survey-grade differential global positioning system (dGPS) surveys of soil surface elevation to detect thaw-related subsidence. papers.title: Integrating Kernel-Based Machine Learning Techniques with Geospatial Analysis for Landslide Susceptibility Mapping in Sikkim, India
papers.source: Journal of Computing in Civil Engineering
papers.summary: Abstract Landslides are among the most destructive natural hazards, causing substantial loss of life and infrastructure, particularly in mountainous regions. Accurate identification of landslide-prone areas remains challenging due to complex and nonlinear interactions among geological, topographical, and environmental factors. This study evaluates kernel-based machine learning approaches, namely, kernel logistic regression (KLR) and support vector machine (SVM), for landslide susceptibility mapping (LSM) in Sikkim, India. A balanced data set comprising 693 landslide and 695 nonlandslide samples was constructed using 15 conditioning factors representing topographic, hydrological, environmental, geological, and seismic conditions. The grid search method was utilized to identify optimal hyperparameter configurations. Model performance was quantitatively assessed using accuracy, kappa coefficient, specificity, area under curve (AUC), landslide density, and success rate curve (SRC). The results demonstrate that the KLR with a polynomial kernel (KLR_poly) achieved the highest predictive performance, with an accuracy of 0.741 and an area under curve (AUC) of 0.829, outperforming other KLR variants, while the SVM with an rbf kernel (SVM_rbf) achieved the highest predictive performance, with an accuracy of 0.749 and an AUC of 0.764, outperforming other SVM variants. Furthermore, the landslide density analysis showed a systematic increase in landslide concentration from low to high susceptibility classes for nonlinear models, while SRC results indicated moderate to good predictive capability across all models, confirming effective spatial prioritization of landslide-prone areas. Additionally, a feature importance analysis was conducted to identify the most significant factors influencing landslide occurrence.

papers.title: Spatial machine learning modelling reveals that soil indicators and tree type best explain shallow landslide release
papers.source: Natural hazards and earth system sciences
papers.summary: The exploration of shallow landslide susceptibility is often impaired by biased landslide inventories, and by over-optimistic performance metrics linked to inadequate models. Here, we use a systematically mapped event inventory of 571 shallow landslides triggered in southern Norway and apply 32 gradient boosted decision tree models to rigorously test the effects of (1) a nested vs. simple cross-validation strategy, (2) spatial vs. non-spatial models, (3) four different cross-validation sampling strategies which were applied on (4) full vs. forest-only datasets. Model evaluation shows that models with random cross-validation provided the highest test performance metrics but did not account for autocorrelation and were likely over-optimistic. The spatial models with spatial cross-validation reduced autocorrelation in the model residuals at the expense of predictive power. Although no model emerged as optimal, findings across models suggest that important explanatory factors like elevation, aspect and bedrock weatherability serve as soil indicators, illustrating a need for improved datasets for soil thickness and heterogeneity. In the forest-only models, tree type was consistently an important predictor, with higher landslide susceptibility in deciduous forest, illustrating the potential of forest variables and forest-specific threshold values in shallow landslide susceptibility mapping.

papers.title: Silent forces rising risks: A systematic review of natural hazards, cascading processes and emerging risk in the Himalaya
papers.source: International Journal of Geography Geology and Environment
papers.summary: Background: The Himalaya is the youngest, highest and most tectonically and climatically active mountain belt on Earth. Hazard prone environments create by large human populations. Traditionally, earthquakes, rainfall- and earthquake triggered landslides, debris flows, glacial lake outburst floods (GLOF), permafrost degradation, rock ice avalanches and snow avalanches have been studied as separate hazard classes. Yet field evidence from recent disasters shows that these events are frequently linked in cascading and compounding sequences. Objective: This review synthesizes peer-reviewed and institutional literature on natural hazards and emerging cascading risk across the Himalayan arc with emphasis on (i) the geological and climatic drivers of individual hazard types (ii) documented cascading and compound hazard pathways, (iii) the growing exposure of settlements and infrastructure and (iv) research and risk management gaps. Methods: A structured systematic literature review was undertaken. Academic search platforms (Google Scholar, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, Wiley Online Library, Nature Portfolio journals, Copernicus/NHESS, MDPI, AGU/Wiley, Frontiers) and institutional repositories (ICIMOD/HKH library, USGS, World Bank, UNDP) were searched using combinations of terms relating to Himalayan hazards, cascading and compound risk, glacial lake outburst floods, seismicity, permafrost and disaster risk reduction for literature published mainly between 2000 and 2026. Because this review draws on open-web-indexed academic search rather than paid bibliographic databases. It is presented as a structured systematic analysis; the eligibility screening, source list and limitations of this approach are stated explicitly in the Methods section. papers.title: Python and Stan code for Bayesian latent-regime analysis of delayed rainfall-induced landslides
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: This software archive contains the Python and Stan source code used for the analyses reported in the Earth's Future manuscript “Latent infiltration regimes mediate environmental controls on delayed rainfall-induced landslides.” The software implements data preprocessing, environmental-control analyses, principal component analysis, soil-thickness and lag-time analyses, predictor–lag relationships, correlation and Mantel analyses, Bayesian latent-regime inference, WAIC-based model selection, posterior predictive checks, regime–soil-thickness analyses, Random Forest and XGBoost environmental attribution, SHAP analysis, and generation of the main and supplementary figures. The Bayesian latent-regime analysis is implemented using Stan and CmdStanPy. Candidate numbers of latent regimes are evaluated using WAIC, with the selected model subsequently used for posterior regime inference and environmental attribution. Version 1.0.0 corresponds to the software release associated with the manuscript submitted to Earth's Future. The software is openly developed at GitHub:https://github.com/liqi1919/Supporting-Materials

papers.title: Empirically informed AHP-FR modeling for multi-hazard susceptibility mapping in a mountainous transport corridors
papers.summary: Abstract Mountainous transport corridors are increasingly exposed to interacting natural hazards that intensify infrastructure, socio-economic, and land-use risks. However, most susceptibility assessments for high-mountain corridors still focus on single hazards or rely heavily on expert-based weighting, which can introduce subjectivity into spatial decision-making. This study develops an empirically informed Analytical Hierarchy Process–Frequency Ratio (AHP-FR) framework for integrated landslide, debris-flow, and flood susceptibility mapping along the Barakhan–Gilgit–Juglot section of the northern China–Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC). The main methodological contribution is the use of frequency-ratio-derived empirical evidence that was integrated with AHP-derived factor weights to calculate final subclass weights and thereby reducing reliance on purely subjective expert judgment. Field surveys, remote sensing datasets, historical hazard inventories, and 12 conditioning factors were integrated in a GIS environment to generate single-hazard susceptibility maps and an eight-class multi-hazard susceptibility map. Independent ROC-AUC validation showed acceptable to very good predictive performance, with AUC values of 0.803 for landslides, 0.762 for debris flows, and 0.872 for floods. The results indicate that 63% of the corridor is exposed to one or more hazards, including 59% exposed to two or more overlapping hazards; 41% are co-susceptible to landslides and debris flows, while 37% falls within the no/very low multi-hazard susceptibility class. The spatial outputs identify major hazard-prone sections, including Attabad, Chalt, and Passu, providing practical guidance for road-maintenance prioritization, slope-stabilization planning, drainage improvement, and emergency preparedness. papers.title: Effects of mapping units on landslide susceptibility assessment: a comparative analysis of slope units and raster cells
papers.summary: The choice of spatial mapping units substantially shapes the accuracy, spatial detail, and interpretability of landslide susceptibility assessment (LSA). To investigate how mapping-unit selection affects LSA performance, this study used Hejing County, Xinjiang, China, as a case study. Based on a historical landslide inventory and a multi-source environmental-factor database, two mapping-unit schemes were constructed: 30 m raster cells and slope units extracted through a hydrology-based delineation method. Based on twelve selected conditioning factors, landslide susceptibility was modeled using four machine-learning algorithms, including logistic regression (LR), multilayer perceptron (MLP), random forest (RF), and XGBoost. In addition, the SHAP method was applied to examine differences in model decision mechanisms and factor contributions between the two mapping-unit schemes. The findings indicate that both mapping-unit schemes are capable of representing the spatial variability of LSA across the study area. The raster-cell-based scheme generally showed better predictive performance, with the mean AUC of the four models increasing from 0.798 under the slope-unit scheme to 0.859 under the raster-cell scheme. This indicates that raster cells are more effective in capturing localized environmental heterogeneity and small-scale high-susceptibility patches. In contrast, the slope-unit-based scheme reduced inter-model performance differences and generated more spatially continuous and stable susceptibility zonation consistent with natural slope boundaries. SHAP analysis further indicates that the dominant conditioning factors were generally consistent between the two schemes; however, raster-cell-based models were more sensitive to localized disturbances and micro-topographic variability, whereas slope-unit-based models emphasized the integrated constraints of geomorphological structure and hydrological processes. papers.title: Dynamic response and damage mechanism of deep overburden layer slope based on shaking table tests
papers.summary: The mountain areas of southwest China are widely covered with loose fractured rock bodies, which are prone to large-scale landslides under seismic action. It is known that the response of the acceleration amplification factor field is closely related to the seismic damage state of the overburden. In order to study the dynamic response and damage mechanism of overburden layer slopes under seismic action, a deep base-covered slope model containing two layers of stacks is used as a prototype in this study, and a series of shaking-table modeling experiments of progressive damage of earthquake-induced slopes are carried out. The cumulative seismic damage deformation process of the slope overburden was identified based on embedded sensors and Particle Image Velocimetry technology, and the energy transfer mechanism of the process was revealed by Hilbert Huang transform. The results show that the non-coherent motion (vibration frequency difference) between the shallow overburden layer-thick overburden layer-bedrock layer is the main controlling factor inducing the slope landslide, and the damage form of the deep overburden slope manifests itself in the form of the trailing edge sliding and extruding the central shear out. The damage starts from the back edge of the slope with increasing seismic intensity and gradually moves toward the middle to lower part of the slope, while extending from the surface to the deeper part of the slope.

Preservation of Isolated Vesicles in Submarine Pumice and Implications for Submarine Slope Stability
papers.summary: Abstract Pumice clasts from submarine eruptions contain abundant isolated vesicles that are completely encased in glass. As erupted clasts cool, gas inside isolated vesicles contracts, leading to low pressures inside those vesicles. Despite low pressures, isolated vesicles can be preserved in submarine pumice deposits to water depths of approximately 1–2 km because the compressive strength of glass exceeds the stresses created by the pressure difference between the inside of gas‐filled vesicles and the ambient pressure. If pumice rafts require abundant isolated vesicles, vents at greater depths are unlikely to form pumice rafts. Fracturing the glass enclosing isolated vesicles during shearing or slope failure would release low pressure vapor, lowering pore pressure and increasing effective stress in the sediment. Pumice‐rich deposits may thus strengthen during shear, making them more gravitationally and seismically stable than other submarine sediments.

Failure Mechanisms in Granular Embankments on Purely Cohesive Clay
papers.summary: Abstract This study adopts an elastic–plastic finite-element approach with strength reduction to investigate the stability of granular embankments over undrained clay, with application to the short-term stability assessment of this embankment at the end of construction. The focus is on the critical dimensionless strength of the foundation at which the failure mechanism will change from deep to translational. It is shown that the critical dimensionless strength is related to the effective friction angle of the embankment layer, the foundation depth ratio, and the slope angle. Comparisons of factors of safety across methods are also made, showing that a deep failure mechanism may lead to unconservative results if the dimensionless strength of the foundation exceeds a critical value.

Improved Gaussian process regression for rock slope displacement monitoring and early warning
papers.summary: Accurate prediction of displacement thresholds and time-to-breach is critical for rock slope stability monitoring. Traditional Gaussian process regression (GPR) lacks probabilistic certainty estimation and adaptability to non-stationary displacement trends, limiting proactive risk management. The proposed displacement threshold certainty estimation (DTCE) method employs a composite kernel (Constant + RBF + White noise), windowed differential analysis of recent measurements, and a hierarchical threshold system to predict breaches in vertical, horizontal, and total displacements. GNSS displacement data from four monitoring points were analysed. 1. DTCE method integrates improved GPR with probabilistic thresholds for displacement breach prediction. 2. Hierarchical thresholds enable 0–100% breach certainty and 0–561.8-day TTB forecasts. 3. Improved GPR achieves MSE ≤ 0.084 mm2, R2 up to 0.991 in slope displacement prediction. 4. Concept drift detection identifies 6.7 mm horizontal displacement divergence in folds.

Assessing agricultural drought intensification and spatiotemporal pattern in the central Rift Valley using multi-source indices
papers.summary: Drought is a complex and multifaceted phenomenon that includes meteorological, agricultural, hydrological, and socio-economic components. Both single and composite drought indices were used in this study to assess agricultural drought in the East Shewa Zone of Central Ethiopia. The Precipitation Condition Index (PCI), Temperature Condition Index (TCI), Vegetation Condition Index (VCI), and Soil Moisture Condition Index (SMCI) were used as single indices. To improve drought characterization, three composite indices—the Scaled Drought Condition Index (SDCI), Vegetation Health Index (VHI), and Optimized Vegetation Dryness Index (OVDI)—were created using empirical weighting and limited optimization techniques. The association of both single and composite indices with the multi-timescale Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI), a widely used meteorological drought measure, was evaluated using in-sample correlation analysis. The results showed that the composite indices (OVDI, VHI, and SDCI) exhibited stronger associations with the multi-timescale SPI than the individual indices, although the strength of these associations varied across seasons and SPI timescales. Among the single indices, the PCI showed the strongest in-sample correlation with the short-term SPI ( r = 0.764 with SPI-1). In contrast, the VCI and SMCI were more strongly correlated with longer-term SPI scales, with SMCI showing in-sample correlations of ( r = 0.577 with SPI-3) and ( r = 0.467 with SPI-6). Spatiotemporal analysis indicated an increase in drought severity, with the area classified as severely dry expanding from 1% to 11% between 2002 and 2015. The findings provide insights into the use of remote sensing indices for drought monitoring and may contribute to the development of improved drought monitoring and early warning approaches in the region.
