Rainfall-Driven Mobilization of Finite Sediment Storage and Two-Phase Debris-Flow Dynamics at Chalk Cliffs
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: This dataset contains the source code and processed model inputs supporting the study “Rainfall-Driven Mobilization of Finite Sediment Storage and Two-Phase Debris-Flow Dynamics at Chalk Cliffs.” The model links rainfall, infiltration, surface-water routing, sediment activation, and subsequent solid–liquid two-phase motion. Sediment activation depends on deposit instability and local surface-water availability. Activated sediment is progressively released from a finite prescribed inventory, with grains and pore water transferred to the moving phases under a saturated-release assumption. Subsequent motion accounts for terrain effects, interphase momentum exchange, liquid-phase Manning resistance, and solid-phase basal friction.The files include the C++ source code, model parameters, processed elevation and parameter rasters, rainfall forcing, and compilation and execution instructions. The supplied configuration represents the 4 July 2014 Chalk Cliffs event in Colorado, USA, using a 5 m grid and a simulation duration of 2000 s. This deposit contains simulation code and processed inputs; raw field observations and full simulation outputs are not included.

papers.title: The greenhouse equipped with 29-mesh insect-proof nets and a zipper door enhances insect pest control and yield of bok choy
papers.summary: Abstract The use of insect-proof nets (IPNs) are an environmentally friendly physical method for preventing insect pests from entering the greenhouse and damaging the vegetables. Bok choy Brassica rapa L. subs. chinensis Brassicaceae, a widely cultivated vegetable in China, is commonly planted in the conventional greenhouses built with plastic films (PFs), IPNs and sliding doors (SDs), and named as PF-SD. However, the effectiveness of controlling agricultural insect pests in PF-SD greenhouse is low due to improper mesh sizes of IPNs and easily-deformative SDs. In this study, the rainproof performance of IPN-ZD greenhouse was compared with that of the open field, and the effects of pest damage, temperature and relative humidity as well as the growth and metabolites of bok choy in the novel greenhouse (IPN-ZD) equipped with 29-mesh IPNs and zipper doors (ZDs) were compared with those of the PF-SD greenhouse at Nanjing, China (31.5°N, 119.0°E) in autumn. The results indicated that the IPN-ZD greenhouse was able to reduce rainfall infiltration compared to that of the open field and increased the yield by 44.9%, reduced internal temperatures, significantly reduced the leaf damage rate from 15.93% to 5.94% and metabolite contents (chlorophyll a and chlorophyll b ) in bok choy compared with those in the PF-SD greenhouse. In conclusion, the IPN-ZD greenhouse could reduce the leaf damage rate, improve the integrity, yield and quality of bok choy and is potentially beneficial to the environment and ecology compared with the PF-SD greenhouse. However, their effectiveness can be affected by inappropriate mesh sizes, inadequate sealing and ventilation conditions. What are the new findings? papers.title: Landfill Leachate Generation, Migration and Impacts on Soil and Groundwater Systems: A Review of Global, African and Nigerian Perspective
papers.source: IIARD INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF GEOGRAPHY AND ENVIRONMENTAL MANAGEMENT
papers.summary: Municipal solid waste generation is rising rapidly worldwide, and in many low- and middle income countries disposal remains dominated by open dumping without engineered containment, creating persistent conditions for the generation and uncontrolled migration of landfill leachate. This review synthesises global, African and Nigerian evidence on the composition, environmental behaviour and public health implications of landfill leachate, with particular attention to humid tropical and Niger Delta settings. Leachate composition is shown to evolve with waste age, climate and landfill design, shifting from organically dominated, high-BOD acidogenic-phase leachate towards ammonia- and chloride-dominated methanogenic-phase leachate over time. Once generated, contaminant transport is governed by the interaction of climate-driven infiltration, subsurface lithology and groundwater flow, conceptualised through the Source-Pathway-Receptor framework and explained mechanistically by Darcy's Law, Toth's groundwater flow system theory and the water balance concept. Empirical studies from Europe, North America, Asia, Africa and Nigeria consistently associate unlined dumpsites with elevated heavy metals, nutrients, organic loading and microbial contamination in soil and groundwater, with health consequences ranging from methemoglobinemia and gastrointestinal disease to chronic heavy-metal toxicity, alongside socio-economic impacts including declining property values and disproportionate exposure of low-income communities. Within the Niger Delta and Port Harcourt specifically, high rainfall, unconsolidated sandy aquifers and shallow groundwater tables create conditions of especially high intrinsic vulnerability. papers.title: Geospatial Assessment of Land Use/Land Cover Dynamics in Wukari–Donga, Taraba State, Nigeria: Implications for Erosion Vulnerability
papers.summary: Land-use/land-cover (LULC) change is an important component of landscape transformation and may influence environmental conditions relevant to soil-erosion vulnerability. This study assessed the spatial and temporal dynamics of LULC in the Wukari–Donga area of Taraba State, Nigeria, for 2000, 2010 and 2024, and examined their potential implications for erosion vulnerability. Multi-temporal Landsat imagery, supported by Sentinel-2 imagery for training-sample identification and verification, was processed in ArcGIS Pro. Seven LULC classes—water, trees/savanna woodland, flooded vegetation, cropland, built-up area, bare ground and rangeland—were mapped using supervised Maximum Likelihood Classification. Area statistics, percentage changes and cross-tabulation were used to assess the spatial extent and temporal dynamics of the classes. In 2024, rangeland was the dominant class, covering 4,249.71 km² (60.94%), followed by cropland (1,285.25 km²; 18.43%) and trees/savanna woodland (1,240.68 km²; 17.79%). Between 2000 and 2024, tree/savanna woodland declined by 52.76% and cropland by 30.66%, whereas rangeland increased by 75.08%. Built-up area, bare ground, flooded vegetation and water bodies increased by 2,077.56%, 3,595.26%, 587.17% and 31.85%, respectively, although the large relative increases in built-up area and bare ground reflected their very small initial extents. LULC change was not uniform: cropland and tree cover increased between 2000 and 2010 but declined substantially during 2010–2024, while rangeland followed the opposite trajectory. The results demonstrate substantial landscape reorganization and identify changes in vegetation, cultivated and exposed surfaces that may influence erosion vulnerability. The findings provide a geospatial basis for sustainable land-use planning and soil-resource management in the Wukari–Donga area.

papers.title: Experimental evaluation of wicking geotextile and grass for moisture control in subgrade with silty clay
papers.summary: After years of operation, subgrade generally equilibrates to a moisture content that is higher than the optimum value. This study explored the influence of geotextile and grass on the moisture reduction and mechanical properties of silty clay. The experimental results showed that installing wicking geotextile effectively reduced the volumetric water content (VWC) by 2% at the monitored depths. By applying another wicking geotextile, the VWC at a depth of 170 mm was reduced further. The combination of grass and geotextile notably optimized the moisture migration, particularly in reducing the VWC around the wicking geotextile. Compared with the control case, the residual matric suction at a depth of 170 mm increased by 12.6, 16.9, and 23.7 kPa in the single-geotextile, double-geotextile, and geotextile–grass cases, respectively. In addition, the single-geotextile case exhibited an average increase of 6.4% in the shear wave velocity (SWV), whereas the geotextile–grass case demonstrated an increase of 9.8%. The higher SWV indicates that the geotextile–grass system helped to mitigate the loss of small-strain stiffness of the silty clay after rainfall infiltration. Furthermore, the high suction at the root–geotextile interface indicates that the geotextile–grass system is an effective approach for improving moisture drainage.

papers.title: Soil and Water Conservation Mechanism in Oil Palm Plantations: A Review of Best Management Practices and Decision Support Strategies
papers.source: WSEAS TRANSACTIONS ON ENVIRONMENT AND DEVELOPMENT
papers.summary: Soil and water conservation on oil palm plantation is increasingly considered as a glimmer of hope for the future sustainability of land functionality and environment. Appropriate management practices and informed decision-making frameworks thus have a strong influence on conservation outcomes. This study aims to systematically identify, categorize, synthesize and quantitatively aggregate peer-reviewed evidence regarding soil and water conservation mechanisms in oil palm plantations, focusing on best management practice strategies and decision support. This study uses Systematic Litigation Review (SLR) the Scopus database is used as a reference in searching scientific publication. A keyword-based structured search was used to identify peer-reviewed articles published from 2020 to 2025 and subsequent screening in sequence based on relevance and language. Thirty-eight articles met all the selection criteria for analysis. Then we extracted data and analyzed it using thematic synthesis with descriptive quantitative aggregation of reported metrics (soil loss, SOC change, runoff reduction, or yield response). The results show six main interrelated themes: control of soil erosion; soil fertility and organic matter management; conservation of water and hydrological regulation; integrated land use and landscape management; agronomic best methods practices; and support for decision-making processes. Quantitative synthesis show that cover-based and structural BMPs decrease soil loss by 50–80%, organic amendments increase SOC by 10–35% and integrated water management decreases runoff by 20–60% across regions reported.

Canopy water delivery and soil physical–hydrological functioning across forest restoration and Eucalyptus stand-development stages in a Cerrado–Atlantic Forest transition
papers.summary: Understanding how vegetation cover, stand development, and prior land-use history are associated with soil physical–hydrological functioning is essential for interpreting runoff regulation in human-modified tropical landscapes. We evaluated rainfall delivery to the soil surface, soil physical condition, infiltration, and surface runoff across five vegetation conditions in a Cerrado–Atlantic Forest transition in southeastern Brazil: a native forest remnant, two enriched restoration stands, and two Eucalyptus plantations representing contrasting stages of stand development and land-use trajectories. Open rainfall and throughfall were monitored over an annual cycle, while soil water content, bulk density, total porosity, soil penetration resistance, infiltration rate, and surface runoff were repeatedly measured in replicated plots. These indicators were further integrated into a standardized Soil Physical Infiltration Potential Index (SPI) to summarize infiltration-favorable versus restrictive soil states. Throughfall increased linearly with rainfall in all vegetation conditions, but cumulative throughfall-to-rainfall ratios differed among covers, indicating contrasting canopy water-delivery patterns. Soil physical indicators showed clearer separation among vegetation conditions than surface runoff alone. The native forest remnant exhibited the most favorable soil conditions, with higher soil water content and total porosity and lower bulk density and penetration resistance, and also showed the highest SPI. In contrast, the younger Eucalyptus stand exhibited the most restrictive conditions and the lowest SPI, while the restoration stands and the 39-month Eucalyptus stand occupied intermediate positions. Seasonal effects were most consistent for soil water content, which was higher during the wet season across all land covers, whereas seasonal changes in bulk density, porosity, and penetration resistance were less uniform. Surface runoff was generally low and highly var

papers.title: Variation of soil physical properties under tea gardens along an alluvial toposequence in Northern Vietnam
papers.summary: Soil structural and hydraulic properties are fundamental for regulating water retention, aeration, saturated hydraulic conductivity (Ks), and root development in perennial cropping systems. This study evaluated the spatial variability of soil physical properties in tea plantation systems developed along contrasting alluvial geomorphic settings in northern Vietnam. The study was conducted along a representative alluvial toposequence in Tan Cuong commune, Thai Nguyen province, including riverside lowlands, previous dikes, and older hillslope positions. Three tea garden sites (TB1, TB2, and TB3) and two adjacent forest sites planted with Acacia spp. (FB1 and FB3) were investigated along the toposequence. An additional tea garden site (TS1) located in Dong Hy commune was included as a comparative site representing a less favorable tea-growing environment developed on different parent materials. Soil samples were collected at two depths (0–10 and 20–30 cm) in triplicate using undisturbed and bulk soil samples for the determination of bulk density, three phase distribution, Ks, aggregate stability expressed as mean weight diameter (MWD), and soil water retention characteristics. The results revealed pronounced differences among sites, depths, and land-use types. Riverside alluvial soils (TB1 and FB1), developed from coarse-textured quartz-rich deposits, exhibited lower MWD values, weaker water retention, and lower structural stability. In contrast, soils located on previous dikes and weathered hillslopes (TB2, TB3, FB3, and TS1) showed higher aggregate stability, more differentiated pore systems, and greater water-holding capacity. At the 20–30 cm depth, TB3 exhibited significantly higher Ks, MWD, and plant-available water than TB1 and TB2 (p < 0.05), indicating more favorable structural and hydraulic conditions. Forest soils generally maintained higher aggregate stability and greater gaseous porosity than adjacent tea soils. The findings demonstrate that soil structural

papers.title: Impact of Soil Data Representation on Streamflow Modelling: A Contiguous-Object Connectivity Approach Case Study in Switzerland
papers.summary: Hydrological models often rely on soil data to represent water partitioning, storage and release within a catchment. However, differences in soil data representation may be obscured by calibration when performance is evaluated primarily against streamflow. This study investigates how alternative soil datasets influence streamflow performance, internal hydrological processes, and parameter sensitivity in a Contiguous-Object Connectivity Approach (COCOA) Soil and Water Assessment Tool Plus (SWAT+) model of an agricultural catchment in Switzerland. Three otherwise identical model setups use a) a global low-resolution soil dataset (World-Soil), b) a national medium-resolution dataset (Swiss-Soil), and c) a high-resolution local soil dataset (Local-Soil). COCOA maintains identical spatial modelling units across scenarios, separating soil-data effects from changes in model discretisation. Before calibration, the three soil scenarios produce pronounced differences in water partitioning: World-Soil produces the greatest surface runoff, Swiss-Soil the greatest subsurface-flow contributions, and Local-Soil the highest evapotranspiration. After calibration, streamflow performance converges, with comparable relative Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency values across scenarios and higher Kling–Gupta efficiency for Swiss-Soil. Nevertheless, contrasting water balance partitioning, soil-water storage, and groundwater-release behaviour persist. Soil-data effects are also more apparent under median- and low-flow conditions than during high flows. These results show that similar outlet-streamflow performance can mask substantial differences in simulated catchment functioning. Soil datasets should therefore be selected according to the intended modelling objective, and internal hydrological diagnostics should complement conventional streamflow-performance metrics.

papers.title: Heterogeneous soils – residual soils
papers.summary: Residual soils formed by physical and chemical weathering processes in situ are heterogeneous soils which vary spatially in properties and composition and vary from completely weathered rock to highly weathered rock. Extensive deposits are found in the tropics but these soils occur in all climatic zones. They can be difficult to sample and test, are partially saturated, have weak bonds, are highly permeable, and exhibit swelling, collapse and loss of strength when subject to changes in effective stress or water content. Properties of residual soils are affected by the test preparation process. Therefore, correlations developed for sedimentary soils may not apply to residual soils. Current properties are not related to stress history since the solids volume decreases as a result of weathering. They can show similar characteristics to overconsolidated soils when loaded but this is due to particle bonding, a result of partial saturation or chemical bonding. They can be in a metastable state which will collapse when sheared, stable-contractive state which causes small strains until yield point when significant straining occurs, or in stable-dilatant state when soil expands when sheared. Residual soil can exhibit fine-grained and coarse-grained behaviour. Collapse of partially saturated residual soils is prevented by controlling infiltration and groundwater. Rainfall induced slope failures are common in residual soils.

papers.title: Modelling soil-root interactions in partly saturated soils: a soil mechanics approach
papers.summary: Soil bioengineering using vegetation is a cost-effective and environmentally sustainable approach for soil stabilisation and enhancing the resilience of civil engineering earthworks. Plants provide hydrological reinforcement to the soil by regulating water content through the evapotranspiration process. Additionally, the presence of root biomass within the soil matrix enhances the soil’s shearing resistance through mechanical entanglement with the surrounding soil. Understanding the hydro-mechanical soil-root interactions is of paramount importance for safe and serviceable geotechnical infrastructure analysis and design. The first phase of this thesis (Chapter 3) focuses on the hydrological soil-root interactions and effects on it. A fully coupled mathematical model is developed to describe the interaction between precipitation, the growing plant root, and the physical properties of the underlying soil layer. A nondimensionalisation technique is used to reduce double-layered soil models to one-layer models by replacing the underlying soil layer with appropriate basal boundary conditions. This model is then used to simulate the spatiotemporal hydro-mechanical response of variably layered vegetated partly saturated soils. The outcomes indicate that root water uptake and porewater pressure interact significantly with the basal boundary condition. Results also suggest that plant roots prevent the development of high water pressures within shallow zones, confirming their importance in maintaining the safety and serviceability of earthwork slopes. The remaining work in this thesis (Chapter 4) focuses on mechanical soil-root interactions with a particular emphasis on the mechanical vulnerability analysis of growing plant roots subject to moisture-driven soil movements. A beam-spring interface model is proposed for the mobilisation of soil resistance and calibrated against pullout experimental data of roots. The analysis incorporated several factors, including the effects o

papers.title: Integrated Irrigation and Disease Management Strategies for Sustainable Wheat Production and Improved Plant Health and Grain Yield
papers.source: Kashmir Journal of Academic Research and Development
papers.summary: Wheat production was expected to provide reliable grain quality and farmer income while using less water and facing climatic variability, soil degradation, disease development, and rising energy costs. This literature-based paper critically synthesized verified research on irrigation, plant disease management, irrigation–disease interactions, sustainability, digital agriculture, and the Pakistan/developing-economy context. It considered irrigation and plant health as related management areas rather than completely separate input decisions. The available evidence did not identify a universal irrigation technology or deficit percentage. Instead, it supported a context-specific approach that considered stored soil water and rainfall, protected important growth stages, managed canopy humidity and nitrogen, used resistant cultivars and clean seed, and applied surveillance, forecasting, and fungicides when justified. Global and China-focused studies reported that moderate deficit or optimized water-saving irrigation could improve water productivity, whereas severe water deficit commonly reduced yield. Jointing/stem elongation was repeatedly identified as an important stage for avoiding water stress, while anthesis and early grain filling were also important when water availability and disease risk required attention. Disease-management evidence emphasized genetic resistance, sanitation, crop rotation, scouting, and forecasting before chemical control. Fusarium head blight required particular attention to weather conditions around anthesis, residue inoculum, cultivar resistance, fungicide timing, and deoxynivalenol risk. Irrigation increased yield without increasing disease in some environments, although dense nitrogen-rich canopies, overhead wetting, and saturated soils could favor foliar diseases and waterlogging. Digital tools were considered decision-support infrastructure that linked observations, analysis, and management actions. Wheat-specific evidence was relativel

papers.title: Impacts of Climate Variability on Infiltration and Groundwater Recharge in the Southeastern Coastal Region of Côte d'Ivoire
papers.summary: This study assesses the impacts of climate variability on infiltration and groundwater recharge within the southeastern coastal corridor of Côte d'Ivoire, spanning from Abidjan to Aboisso. The methodology integrates the Pettitt test to detect rainfall stationarity breaks, followed by water balance modeling using the Thornthwaite and Tixeront–Berkaloff methods to quantify infiltration. The analysis relies on a multi-decadal meteorological dataset, including a 54-year rainfall series (1960–2014) and a 43-year temperature record (1971–2014), coupled with a 23-year historical groundwater level monitoring dataset (1982–2005) obtained from deep boreholes. precipitation fluctuations were correlated with piezometric level variations across 30 shallow wells and 9 deep boreholes. The results identify a critical regional rainfall break occurring in 1982. Annual infiltration available for aquifer recharge ranged from 0 mm to maximum values of 856 mm, 998 mm, and 1011 mm at the Adiaké, Abidjan-Airport, and Bingerville synoptic stations, respectively. Prior to the 1982 break, mean infiltration rates (456 mm, 437 mm, and 378 mm, respectively) exceeded runoff (300 mm, 292 mm, and 285 mm), accounting for over 55% of the total rainfall surplus (infiltration + runoff). Post-1982, infiltration significantly decreased, dropping to between 20% and 40% of the surplus. Consequently, piezometric heads in deep aquifers (30 to 90 m depth) declined by 1.3 to 5.3 m, with borehole recharge occurring exclusively when the preceding year's rainfall exceeded 1,750 mm. In contrast, shallow wells (water table depth: 0.45 to 12.46 m) exhibited near-instantaneous recharge responses following rainfall events. Beyond quantifying volumetric variations, the scientific implications of these findings highlight a structural transition in the regional hydrological regime. The climate-driven reduction in natural infiltration, amplified by land surface modifications, compromises the long-term sustainability of th

papers.title: Contribution of soil coarse fragments to plant available water
papers.summary: Stony soils are widespread and used for food production, but the effect of coarse fragments (CFs) on water retention remains poorly understood. This study aimed to assess whether the available water (AW) retained in CFs depends on their size and porosity. CFs from three contrasting sites in southern Brazil, varying in size and porosity, were analyzed. Measurements included their volume, total porosity, bulk density, and water retention at suctions of 1 m and 150 m. AW was estimated as the difference of water retention between suctions of 1 m and 150 m. For each site, linear regression was used to evaluate the relationship of AW in CFs with total porosity, water-filled porosity at 1 m suction (θ 1m ), and volume of CFs. Results showed that AW in soil coarse fragments (CFs) depends almost exclusively on their porosity (R 2 around 0.99), while CF size has a negligible effect (R 2 ≤ 0.10). Compared to CFs total porosity, the CFs water-filled porosity at a suction of 1 m is a slightly better predictor of AW in CFs, but the total porosity of CFs is advantageous because its determination is less laborious and equipment-dependent. The relationship between AW and porosity in CFs depends on CFs parent rock lithology and weathering degree, which implies in calibration demands of a pedofunction type AW (porosity).

papers.title: A case study on SWMM based evaluation of rain barrel and downspout disconnection scenarios for urban stormwater management
papers.summary: Colombo, the executive and judicial capital of Sri Lanka, is located on the southwestern coast of the country and has experienced rapid urbanization in recent years, driven by infrastructure development, land use changes, and the growing impacts of climate change. These factors have significantly increased the frequency and severity of urban flooding. Therefore, this study explores the stormwater management problems in the 686.3-hectare study catchment, adjacent to the Kelani River in suburban Colombo, and proposes effective stormwater management strategies to avoid flooding in the area. Using GIS-based analysis, the study area was divided into 36 sub-catchments to determine the elevation and imperviousness characteristics of the study area and generate a Digital Elevation Model (DEM). Additionally, land use and land cover (LULC) mapping and change detection analysis were carried out using ArcGIS. The obtained spatial data were used in the EPA-SWMM model to evaluate stormwater responses under different rain barrel-based LID scenarios. Three scenarios were evaluated: the existing condition (no LID), rain barrel with downspout connection (No Disconnect), and rain barrel with downspout disconnection (Disconnect). The runoff coefficients for the baseline scenario were 0.849 and 0.871 for the 2-year and 10-year storms, respectively. The rain barrel with-disconnect scenario reduced these to 0.379 and 0.456, while the no-disconnect scenario resulted in 0.563 and 0.598, respectively. The Disconnect configuration proved most effective in reducing average total runoff by 55% and 48% for the 2-year and 10-year storms, respectively, while more than doubling infiltration rates. In contrast, the No Disconnect configuration provided only moderate runoff reduction through temporary storage, without meaningfully restoring natural infiltration processes. Moreover, Outfall loading was 196.15 and 234.28 L under existing conditions for the 2- and 10-year storms, respectively. The discon

papers.title: Towards Sustainable Mine Restoration: Environmental Safety Assessment of Phosphorus Migration Following Sewage Sludge Compost Application to Abandoned Phosphate Mines in Southwestern China
papers.summary: Repurposing waste-derived organic amendments for degraded land restoration supports the transition toward a circular economy, yet the associated environmental risks must be rigorously evaluated to ensure long-term sustainability. Sewage sludge compost (SSC) is a promising soil amendment for the ecological restoration of abandoned phosphate-mine sites (APMSs). However, SSC application may alter phosphorus (P) migration and release, thereby posing a risk of secondary pollution that could undermine the sustainability of mine reclamation efforts. Here, dynamic leaching-column experiments simulating three years of natural rainfall infiltration were conducted to investigate P-release characteristics under different fertilization scenarios, including application rate, application method, and compost maturity. Ecological risk was evaluated using a modified phosphorus pollution index (PPI), and the likely mechanisms governing P leaching and release in APMS soils were explored. Dissolved reactive P was the predominant released form in all treatments, accounting for 67.9–85.6% of total released P. Increasing the SSC application rate reduced the cumulative total phosphorus (TP) release ratio (on a soil TP content basis) from 0.0348% in the unfertilized control to 0.0264–0.0299%. Deep full-profile incorporation within the upper 20 cm of APMS soil and subsurface application reduced TP release by 36.8% and 34.1%, respectively, relative to shallow full-profile incorporation within the upper 10 cm of APMS soil. Primary sewage sludge compost (SSC*) controlled P release only when cumulative rainfall infiltration was ≤669 mm; by the third year, the ecological risk increased from slight to the severe-pollution level. SSC applied at 120 t ha−1 under the shallow full-profile fertilization mode reduced the PPI of APMS1 and APMS2 by 30.8–44.8% and 5.6–12.3%, respectively. P dissolution was positively associated with Ca release. Humic substances likely formed larger, less mobile, non-rigid c

papers.title: The Effect of Climate Change and Land Use Change Scenarios on the Design Flood Discharge and the Curve Number: The Case of the Noelmina and Benanain Watersheds, Indonesia
papers.summary: Climate change substantially alters watershed hydrology, primarily through increased flood discharge. This study uses the Hydrologic Engineering Center’s Hydrologic Modeling System (HEC-HMS) to assess how climate change and land-use change scenarios affect the design flood discharge and Curve Number (CN) for the Noelmina and Benanain watersheds in East Nusa Tenggara, Indonesia. The Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs) 2.6 and 8.5 were applied for the periods 2041-2060 and 2081-2100. The simulated flood discharge increased progressively over time, most notably under the high-emission RCP 8.5 scenario towards the end of the century. Compared with the discharge from observed rainfall in 2024, the 25-year design flood under RCP 8.5 (2081-2100) increased by 35.6% in Noelmina and 32.6% in Benanain, while the 50-year flood increased by 36.3% and 30.7%, respectively. A land-use analysis conducted between 2015 and 2024 revealed the conversion of vegetated land into residential and agricultural areas. This raised the composite CN from 83.19 to 83.73 in Noelmina and from 85.99 to 86.82 in Benanain. This indicates a reduction in infiltration capacity and an increase in surface runoff. The combined effects of climate change and land use are likely to exacerbate future flood risk, highlighting the need for integrated watershed management and adaptive mitigation strategies.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence applications in porous asphalt pavement
papers.source: Bulletin of Electrical Engineering and Informatics
papers.summary: Porous asphalt pavement (PAP) was developed as a sustainable pavement solution to improve rainwater infiltration, reduce inundation, and improve driving safety. The performance of PAP is influenced by the complex interactions between pore structures, clogging mechanisms, and structural and thermal responses, thus encouraging the application of artificial intelligence (AI) in its modeling. This study aims to comprehensively synthesize the application of AI in PAP through the systematic literature review (SLR) approach. The SLR process was carried out against the publication of the 2021–2026 period from the Elsevier, SpringerLink, and MDPI databases, which resulted in 10 high-quality articles for analysis. The results show that AI enables accurate and non-destructive prediction of hydraulic and clogging performance, while AI-integrated mechanistic models achieve a correlation coefficient of up to 0.994 for structural response and an error below 5% for thermal conductivity. Image-based deep learning and generative models further demonstrate potential for pavement condition assessment and porous microstructure modeling. The novelty of this review lies in integrating evidence on AI applications across the hydraulic, clogging, structural, thermal, and microstructural domains of PAP. The findings highlight the need for an integrated, material-specific AI framework to support sustainable PAP design, monitoring, and maintenance.

Flood Risk Assessment in Urban Environments: Dynamic Modeling and Multi-Scenario Analysis
papers.source: Journal of Geology Geography and Geoecology
papers.summary: Urban flooding has become one of the most significant challenges for rapidly urbanizing cities, where intensive land development, increasing impervious surfaces, and complex topography substantially amplify surface runoff and flash flood hazards. The aim of this study is to develop an integrated methodological framework for assessing urban flood risk through dynamic hydrological modelling and multi-scenario spatial analysis using Geographic Information Systems. The study was conducted within a highly urbanized micro-catchment located in the Yasamal district of Baku, Azerbaijan, characterized by steep relief, predominantly impermeable clay soils, and dense urban development. The methodology combines Digital Elevation Model analysis, land use and land cover assessment, hydrological soil classification, the Rational and Soil Conservation Service Curve Number methods, runoff concentration modelling based on the National Resources Conservation Service Kinematic Wave approach, and Geographic Information Systems-based spatial analysis. Rainfall scenarios ranging from 1 to 100 mm were simulated to evaluate runoff generation, peak discharge, flood propagation, and the spatial distribution of flood hazards at the individual building level. The results demonstrate that the interaction between relief morphology, intensive urbanization, and low soil infiltration capacity creates favourable conditions for rapid stormwater accumulation and flash flood formation. Approximately 79% of the total runoff is concentrated within three critical topographic depressions, while floodwaters reach the most vulnerable buildings within only 3.0–4.3 minutes under high-intensity rainfall scenarios. Comparative analysis revealed that the Rational method provides more reliable estimates of peak discharge and runoff concentration time, whereas the Soil Conservation Service Curve Number method more accurately predicts runoff volume. Their combined application significantly improves the reliability of

papers.title: Explainable Machine Learning-Based Multi-Hazard Risk Assessment and Upazila-Level Intervention Prioritization in the Chattogram Region, Bangladesh
papers.summary: The increasing occurrence of natural hazards, either individually or in combination, has intensified disaster risk worldwide, with the Chattogram Region of Bangladesh representing a prominent multi-hazard hotspot where earthquakes, landslides, and floods frequently coexist. An interpretable GIS–ML-based multi-hazard risk assessment (MHRA) framework was developed to generate earthquake, landslide, and flood susceptibility zones (EQSZ, LSSZ, and FSZ) using ensemble machine learning algorithms, with model predictions explained through SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). The resulting susceptibility maps were integrated into a Multi-Hazard Index, which was then combined with a Vulnerability Index to produce the final Multi-Hazard Risk Zone (MHRZ). GBM achieved the highest predictive performance for earthquake (AUC = 0.799) and landslide (AUC = 0.786), whereas RF performed best for flood susceptibility (AUC = 0.917). SHAP identified shear-wave velocity (Vs30), Soil Moisture Index, and elevation as the most influential predictors of earthquake, landslide, and flood susceptibility, respectively. Although the eastern hill districts exhibited the highest multi-hazard susceptibility, the MHRZ identified the densely populated upazilas of Chattogram and Cox's Bazar as the highest-risk areas because socio-economic vulnerability outweighed comparatively moderate hazard susceptibility. Approximately 55.10% of the study area fell within the very low to low-risk classes, whereas only 21.49% fell within the high-to-very-high-risk classes, highlighting the critical role of socio-economic vulnerability in shaping regional disaster risk. The proposed MHRA framework offers a methodologically transferable basis for evidence-based disaster risk reduction (DRR) by enabling upazila-level policy screening, preliminary DRR intervention prioritization, and resilient spatial planning in multi-hazard, data-scarce regions.

papers.title: Water Balance Viewer (Esri), Embedded in GeoHub
papers.summary: A water balance viewer embedded in the Meghalaya State GeoHub, credited to Esri Hydro, showing for any clicked location how rainfall divides between runoff, evaporation and infiltration and how that changes over time. Useful for looking at the modelled water balance at one place at a time and for presentations. It yields no table or downloadable figures.

papers.title: A well-balanced local radial basis functions collocation method for single-layer and two-layer shallow water flows with rainfall and infiltration
Deep soil desiccation patterns and ecohydrological feedbacks of vegetation re-establishment in desiccated soils on the Loess Plateau
papers.summary: Deep soil water (>200 cm) is a critical water source for sustaining vegetation productivity and long term ecosystem stability in water limited regions. However, under the large scale “Grain for Green” program on the Loess Plateau, deep soil water patterns across different vegetation restoration types remain insufficiently understood. The ecohydrological feedbacks associated with vegetation reestablishment in desiccated soils are also unclear. This study integrated 6,516 observations from 176 sites across the Loess Plateau. We systematically assessed soil water conditions and desiccation characteristics within 0–1000 cm soil profiles under rainfed cropland, natural grassland, artificial grassland, orchards, and ecological forests (including tree and shrub plantations). In addition, a 5-year replanting experiment was conducted on soils with pre-existing deep desiccation (>10 m). The experiment compared the coupled responses of soil water dynamics and plant growth under different vegetation configurations. The results show that deep soil desiccation is widespread during vegetation restoration on the Loess Plateau. Rainfed orchards, ecological forests, and artificial grasslands developed persistent dry layers 3–5 m thick. The most severe desiccation occurred in ecological forests. Following replanting on desiccated soils, deep rooted species ( Robinia pseudoacacia L., Caragana korshinskii Kom., and Medicago sativa L.) continuously depleted middle and deep soil water because of their high water consumption. They also preferentially utilized infiltrated rainfall, thereby limiting deep recharge and maintaining or exacerbating soil desiccation. Meanwhile, these species exhibited a rainfall-pulse-driven adaptive growth strategy that supported survival and biomass accumulation. In contrast, shallow rooted vegetation ( Poa annua L.) and bare land showed limited utilization of deep soil water. Their low water consumption facilitated downward rainfall infiltration. This promoted

papers.title: Comparative evaluation of frequency ratio and index of entropy models for landslides susceptibility mapping of Dikhow river basin, Northeast India
papers.summary: Landslide Susceptible Mapping is a significant approach in hilly regions for delineating the potential areas for landslide occurrence. North-eastern states of India are most prone to landslides due to intense monsoonal rainfall, complex geology, and increasing anthropogenic activities. A significant portion of the Dikhow River Basin lies within the hilly regions of Nagaland, where intense monsoonal rainfall and fragile geological conditions trigger slope instability. Numerous reported landslide incidents highlight the severity of this disaster in this region. This research focuses on the comparative assessment of two landslide susceptibility maps generated from two bivariate models, namely (i) Frequency Ratio (FR) and (ii) Index of Entropy (IOE), in the Dikhow River Basin by integrating 12 landslide triggering factors and 632 landslide inventories using Geospatial Technology. The generated Landslide Susceptibility Map has been categorized into five hierarchical classes, from very low to very high, using the natural-break classification system. The study indicated that 19.9% and 8.4% of the study area correspond to very high susceptibility to landslides by FR and IOE, respectively. The validation results illustrated satisfactory performance for both models with AUC values of 0.81 and 0.79 for the training datasets, and 0.82 and 0.8 for the testing datasets, respectively. R-index values indicate that 64.81% (FR) and 60.25% (IOE) of landslide occurrences were associated with very high susceptibility classes. The validation process reveals that the FR has better success in comparison to the IOE model. In order to reduce the negative effects of landslide hazards, the suggested research will assist government, policymakers, and decision-makers in managing and mitigating the adverse consequences of landslides.

papers.title: Porous Media Free-Flow Coupling - From REV to Pore Scale and Back
papers.summary: Flow and transport processes in domains composed of a porous medium and an adjacent free-flow region appear in a wide range of industrial, bio-medical and environmental applications. Industrial applications range from flow in fuel cells to drying processes; possible bio-medical applications include the interplay of distribution processes in blood vessels and in the surrounding tissue. Applications in environmental systems include infiltration of overland flow during rainfall, groundwater contamination due to infiltrating pollutants and evaporation from soil. One of the key challenges for coupled free flow and porous-medium flow arises from the fact that the overall effective behaviour depends strongly on interface processes that occur on small spatial scales (pore scale), although the overall system of interest is often too large to resolve these processes explicitly in detail. REV-scale models are usually not able to capture all the relevant physical processes for such coupled systems. For the accurate description of interface phenomena, it is therefore necessary to develop model concepts that combine information gained through pore-scale and REV-scale models. The first part of the lecture includes the following items: -an explanation of relevant processes of mass, momentum and energy transfer at the interface between a free-flow and a porous-media system; -a presentation of conceptual models for coupled single-phase free flow and two-phase porous-medium flow with a detailed description of the models in the free flow and in the porous medium for the pore and REV scale; -comparison studies to show the advantages and disadvantages in relation to classical approaches; the coupling concepts are discussed on the basis of different technical or environmental issues. In the second part of the lecture I would very much like to discuss the results on the basis of various detailed use cases. papers.title: Assessing the hydrological water balance of the poorly gauged semi-arid Oued Cherraa basin in northeastern Morocco using the SWAT model
papers.summary: Water resources management in semi-arid areas is facing increasing difficulties, which include climatic variability, excessive use of groundwater resources, and poor hydrometeorological network coverage, over-extraction of groundwater resources, and poor hydrometeorological network coverage. The main objective of this research is to apply the SWAT Water Budget module in estimating the hydrological water balance of the poorly gauged basin of Oued Cherraa in the Moulouya watershed in northeastern Morocco. It aims at quantifying the main components of the water balance: precipitation, evapotranspiration (ET), surface runoff, and groundwater recharge, on the one hand. On the other one, it is about analyzing their spatial variability in a data-scarce context. The SWAT model was implemented using available climatic data and daily discharge data from one hydrometric station called Tazarhine. The model was calibrated and validated using the SUFI-2 algorithm within the SWAT-CUP interface. The accuracy of the model simulation was considered to be acceptable due to the efficiency values of Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency being 0.58 and 0.60 for calibration and validation, respectively, as well as the percentage bias being minimal at − 9.1% and − 0.2%, also for calibration and validation, respectively. Moreover, sensitivity analysis indicated that the most influential parameters to the simulations are RCHRG_DP, ALPHA_BF and CN2. From water balance analysis, evapotranspiration is estimated to be responsible for almost 89% of precipitation, while surface runoff is less than 6%. Recharge of shallow aquifers is much more significant compared to recharge of deep aquifers, while irrigated areas demonstrate groundwater depletion. It is evident from these results that groundwater resources available in semi-arid areas where there is no adequate monitoring system are quite fragile, which proves the importance of SWAT as a decision-support tool.

papers.title: Friction over gravitational forcing: Disentangling the controls of Hortonian overland flow and erosion through energy-centred process modelling
papers.summary: Abstract. This study investigates the coupled dynamics of Hortonian overland flow (HOF) and sediment transport observed during rainfall simulations at the plot scale using the process-based Catflow model with an energy centred approach. A hierarchical calibration strategy was applied to reproduce overland flow generation, flow velocities in sheet and rill domains and sediment detachment sequentially, allowing the dominant controls on HOF and erosion processes to be identified. The results show that antecedent soil moisture and surface roughness are the primary controls on HOF generation, whereas rainfall intensity and slope had no significant effect within the investigated range. Increasing surface roughness reduced surface runoff and total sediment export, while simultaneously increasing the ratio between rill and sheet flow velocities, indicating enhanced flow concentration into preferential pathways. No clear relationship was observed between flow velocities and slope, demonstrating that overland flow dynamics are primarily limited by friction rather than gravitational forcing. The model reproduced overland flow generation, flow partitioning and total eroded sediment with good consistency. The results indicate that sheet flow primarily governs sediment detachment and energy dissipation, whereas rills function as efficient sediment transport pathways. Increasing surface roughness promoted flow concentration into rills, where the greater hydraulic radius reduced relative frictional losses and enabled a more efficient conversion of potential into kinetic energy. Consequently, downslope kinetic energy transport became increasingly dominant within the rill domain, while the overall system remained friction dominated. This energetic interpretation links overland flow generation, flow organisation and erosion dynamics through the balance between energy input, dissipation and redistribution. Overall, the study highlights the importance of frictional resistance as prime l

Revisión de medidas para la mitigación de inundaciones implementando sistemas urbanos de drenaje sostenible y obras grises
papers.summary: The rapid increase in soil impermeability due to urban expansion, coupled with growing rainfall, causes flooding that affects residential homes, university campuses, and municipalities. Urban growth outpaces conventional storm drainage systems, which were designed with limited capacity, restricting infiltration and aquifer recharge, leading to increased surface runoff and high flood risks. This review synthesizes the implementation of Sustainable Urban Drainage Systems (SuDS) and grey infrastructure as a comprehensive approach. Flood scenarios and environmental issues in Latin America and worldwide were analyzed, proposing selection criteria with advantages and disadvantages for both measures. Additionally, key co-benefits related to health, human well-being, water quality improvement, environmental care, and enhanced urban landscaping are discussed. Finally, a guiding matrix was created summarizing the essential applicability of each type of SuDS and grey infrastructure, serving as a decision-making tool for urban planning, educational institutions, and engineering in general.

papers.title: Influence of Geogrid-Geotextile Reinforcement on Field-Derived Soil-Water Characteristic Curves and Climate-Driven Moisture Dynamics of Compacted Clay Slopes
papers.summary: Geosynthetic reinforcement is widely used to improve slope stability; however, its association with soil–water characteristic curve (SWCC) behavior under natural climatic exposure remains insufficiently understood. This study compared two geometrically identical outdoor reduced-scale compacted-clay slope models: one containing three geogrid-integrated geotextile layers and one unreinforced control. Sensors at a depth of 0.46 m recorded volumetric water content (VWC) and matric suction at 15-min intervals. Drying-path van Genuchten curves were evaluated over the common reliable suction domain of 5.0–51.1 kPa using a trailing 24-h classification and 2000 paired calendar-day bootstrap resamples. The reinforced curve remained above the control curve throughout this domain. The median reinforced-minus-control VWC difference decreased from 0.0454 m3/m3 at 5 kPa (95% conditional interval: 0.0351–0.0590) to 0.0126 m3/m3 at 51.1 kPa (0.0074–0.0180). This difference persisted across 182 sensitivity configurations, although individual model parameters were weakly identifiable. Across 21 rainfall events of at least 5 mm, the reinforced model exhibited smaller median VWC increases and suction decreases. These results provide quantitative benchmarks for interpreting and modeling hydraulic responses in reinforced clay systems. Because only one model represented each configuration and mechanical performance was not measured, the findings are conditional and do not establish a replicated reinforcement effect or improved slope stability.

Land-use controls on soil hydraulic functioning: the role of pore organization and gravel distribution in an agricultural catchment
papers.summary: Soil hydraulic functioning in headwater catchments reflects interactions among pore organization, land use, and coarse-fragment distribution, but the relative importance of these controls remains uncertain when point measurements are interpreted at broader spatial scales. This study evaluated how near-surface soil permeability and water storage varied among land-use and tillage systems and whether those variations were associated with soil structure and gravel distribution in a 1.19 km 2 agricultural headwater catchment in southern Brazil. Physical and hydraulic properties were measured in the 0–0.05 m layer at 69 sampling points (414 undisturbed cores), including bulk density, pore-size distribution, saturated hydraulic conductivity (Ksat), air permeability (Ka), water retention across matric potentials, gravel content, texture, and soil organic carbon (SOC). Planned contrasts, Pearson correlations, and principal component analysis (PCA) were used to evaluate group differences and multivariate associations. Natural forest had lower bulk density and greater permeability-related attributes than grazed grassland, whereas conservation tillage increased water retention and plant-available water relative to conventional tillage without a consistent increase in Ksat. Gravel abundance was positively associated with macroporosity, Ka, and Ksat and negatively associated with water retention near field capacity, but these correlations do not establish a causal pathway. Land-use differences in water retention were strongest near saturation and diminished at higher suctions. The first two PCA axes explained 49.3% of total variance and separated transmission-related attributes (Ksat, Ka, macroporosity, total porosity, and saturated water content) from denser, storage-related conditions, while substantial variability remained in higher components. Overall, near-surface hydraulic functioning was more closely associated with pore organization and coarse-fragment abundance than with

papers.title: Soil Cracking in Vertisols: Mechanism, Impacts and Management Strategies
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Black cotton soil (Vertisols) exhibit pronounced surface cracking due to their high content of smectite‐rich clay minerals, which experiences intense shrink‐swell cycles during alternating wetting and drying conditions. These dynamic structural changes lead to the formation of deep and interconnected cracks, significantly influencing the soil structure, water infiltration, runoff generation, soil loss and overall soil stability. Consequently, the adoption of different sustainable soil and water management practices that regulate soil moisture regimes which is essential for minimizing surface cracking and enhancing the resilience of Vertisols under variable rainfall conditions. The results revealed that these management practices substantially reduced key cracking parameters, i.e., crack depth, width, length, area and volume ranging from 3.60%–40.6%, 3.80%–46.2%, 4.40%–41.4%, 5.80%–57.0% and 18.0%–74.0%, respectively. In addition to their effects on surface cracking, agronomic, biological and soil structural management practices resulted in marked reductions in runoff (3.30%–98.3%; 1.31–39.0 mm) and soil loss (2.30%–99.7%; 0.23–9.80 t ha −1 ) while enhancing water‐use efficiency (WUE) by up to 22.1%. Similarly, hydrological and land‐configuration practices, including broad‐bed and furrow systems, ridge‐furrow configurations, bunding and farm ponds reduced runoff by 6.44%–75.5% (1.65–26.8 mm), soil loss by 10.9%–98.0% (0.063–9.60 t ha −1 ) and improved WUE by 3.40%–41.5%. Inclusively, this review elucidates the mechanisms governing cracking behaviour in Vertisols and underscores the critical role of soil and water management practices in mitigating surface cracking, reducing runoff and soil loss and sustaining soil health. Therefore, the adoption of these practices is therefore vital for enhancing crop productivity and long‐term land resilience in semiarid and arid regions.

papers.title: Evolution Process and Failure Mechanism of a Multi‐Factor Coupled Loess Landslide: A Case Study in Xiangning County, China
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Loess landslides are major geohazards on the Chinese Loess Plateau, where rainfall and engineering activities commonly trigger slope failures that also drive slope‐to‐gully evolution. This study investigates the ZQ landslide (23 April 2023) in Xiangning County, Shanxi Province, using field surveys, UAV photogrammetry, SBAS‐InSAR, dynamic triaxial tests and finite‐element simulations to clarify deformation, material behaviour, geomorphic evolution and failure mechanisms. The landslide (200 m long, 308 m wide; 6.0 × 10 4 m 2 ) developed in a Quaternary loess–palaeosol sequence and showed episodic retrogression, producing three rear scarps. The sliding mass moved from one side of the gully toward the valley bottom, where the deposit partially occupied the gully and induced frontal bulging, showing local adjustment of the gully. SBAS‐InSAR revealed central displacement accumulation with peak line‐of‐sight displacement of −43.3 mm and a mean rate of −41 mm/year; deformation acceleration coincided with rainfall, especially the 71.6 mm total in April 2023. Dynamic triaxial tests show that saturated loess is sensitive to cyclic loading. Higher CSR and loading frequency accelerated plastic‐strain accumulation and dynamic strength degradation, providing laboratory evidence for cyclic‐load–induced weakening. Scenario‐based finite‐element modelling indicated progressive weakening under sustained rainfall. Under the coupled rainfall–vibration scenario, deformation became more toe‐controlled, with a maximum horizontal displacement of 4.28 m, toe uplift of 4.10 m and a factor of safety of 0.773. The development of a connected plastic zone indicates progressive failure and potential reactivation. The results suggest that rainfall‐driven infiltration softening within the loess–palaeosol stratigraphic structure was the main hydrological trigger, whereas mining‐related disturbance may have contributed to failure by promoting crack development, deformation accumulation and cyc

papers.title: Analisis Risiko Bencana Kekeringan Menggunakan Metode Kerawanan (Hazard), Kerentanan (Vulnerability) Dan Kapasitas (Capacity) Di Kelurahan Cilembang Kota Tasikmalaya
papers.summary: Drought is a hydrometeorological disaster that can threaten water availability and increase the vulnerability of urban communities. This study aims to analyze drought disaster risk in Cilembang Village, Tasikmalaya City, based on hazard, vulnerability, and capacity components. A descriptive approach combined with spatial analysis based on secondary data was employed. Hazard was assessed using rainfall, slope, soil type, geological structure, and land-use parameters; vulnerability covered economic, social, and environmental dimensions; while capacity was evaluated based on community and institutional preparedness. Each parameter was classified and scored, and the components were subsequently integrated through an overlay technique using ArcGIS 10.8. The results indicate that Cilembang Village has high drought hazard and vulnerability levels, influenced by low rainfall according to the classification applied in this study, the dominance of residential land use of approximately 90%, high population density, and limited water infiltration areas. Institutional capacity is already present; however, drought-specific early warning systems and community participation still require strengthening. The integration of hazard, vulnerability, and capacity indicates that Cilembang Village is classified as having a high drought risk. These findings emphasize the importance of water conservation, sustainable land-use management, and strengthening community capacity as key components of drought risk reduction strategies.

papers.title: Cloud computing and global satellite products for potential groundwater recharge estimation: application to the Basin of Mexico
papers.summary: Groundwater recharge (GWr) estimation is fundamental for assessing aquifer storage changes, ensuring groundwater sustainability, and supporting effective water management. However, regional groundwater recharge assessment remains challenging because it requires integrating large geospatial datasets, computational resources, and hydrogeological information that are often unavailable in data-limited regions. This study presents a cloud-based framework for estimating potential groundwater recharge (GWpr) using open satellite products and the Thornthwaite-Mather (T-M) water balance model implemented in Google Earth Engine (GEE) and executed through Google Colab. The framework integrates globally available datasets, including CHIRPS precipitation, MODIS potential evapotranspiration, and OpenLandMap soil properties, within a reproducible Python workflow that minimizes dependence on local computational infrastructure. The Basin of Mexico (BM), an endorheic volcanic basin affected by intensive groundwater exploitation, was selected as a case study to evaluate the framework against a previously calibrated Soil Water Balance (SWB) model. The proposed implementation estimated a mean annual ground water potential recharge (GWpr) of ~ 44.7 mm/year, closely matching the reference model at the basin scale. Differences between both approaches were ~ 4–5% in the Zona Metropolitana and Tecocomulco groundwater management units (GMUs), whereas larger discrepancies (~ 20–30%) occurred in eastern and northern GMUs, reflecting differences in model temporal representation and local hydroclimatic conditions. Overall, the proposed cloud-computing framework provides an accessible, reproducible, and transferable approach for estimating GWpr using globally available datasets, facilitating groundwater assessments in data-limited regions with diverse hydrogeological settings.

papers.title: Mechanics of Fungi-Induced Biocementation in Soils and Rocks
papers.summary: Nature-based engineered processes, such as microbes, enzymes, biopolymers, and most recently fungi, have emerged as effective solutions for ground improvement by altering the mechanical behavior of geomaterials. Among these approaches, fungi have attracted growing interest due to their ability to form interconnected mycelial networks that modify pore structure while remaining metabolically active across diverse environmental conditions; however, the if , how , and why fungi modify the mechanical behavior of geomaterials (soils and rock) underground, from near-surface (soils) to deeper (bedrock and rock masses) strata, remains unexplored. Therefore, this novel study investigates the mechanical response (compressive strength, UCS ) and microstructural characteristics across both rocks and soils modified by fungal-induced biocementation and further explores the potential of engineered fungal biocementation for ground improvement across underground strata of soils and bedrock. Treatment was conducted using the fungus Trichoderma virens under two treatment regimes for 10 days, spore-dominant and nutrient-dominant fungal-inoculation conditions, to assess how spore density or nutrient availability influences fungal growth and geomaterial modification. Next, uniaxial compression tests were conducted on treated and untreated soil and rock specimens, and microstructural analyses were performed to characterize the geomaterial changes due to fungal biocementation within the pore networks. Results show that while fungal biocementation enhanced rock strength ( UCS ), with improvements up to +12% and +15% under spore-dominant and nutrient-dominant conditions, respectively, the soil UCS after treatment exhibited variable and more complex responses. Individual soil specimens showed heterogeneous reinforcement due to oxygen-limited fungal colonization at soil specimen depth, with some specimens showing increased strength and others remaining comparable to controls. Nevertheless, the

papers.title: Changes in the annual cycle in shallow subarctic groundwater regimes over 50 years
papers.summary: Seasonal groundwater level regimes are exposed to climate change, with implications for drought and flood risks, water supply, agriculture, and ecosystems. Changes in the intra-annual groundwater fluctuations are accentuated in quickly responding shallow aquifers found worldwide, but particularly in subarctic regions, where the cold winter season attenuates infiltration and evaporation. To identify the types of subarctic groundwater regimes and their responses to the changing climate, 50-year groundwater level data from 52 monitoring stations throughout Finland were analyzed. This was done by partitioning around medians (PAM) clustering of Pearson correlations and a principal component analysis (PCA) of normalized monthly values. Four distinct regimes were identified, mostly following the southwest–northeast temperature and snow condition gradients. The migration of regimes towards the colder northeastern regions could be seen between the clustering periods of 1975–1999 and 2000–2024. This migration manifested as rising winter levels and lowering summer levels, in addition to changing seasonality timing, such as the spring recharge peak advancing by an average of half a month and by up to two months. Furthermore, seasonal groundwater level responses were seen to depend on the projected surface area of the aquifer, as comparatively larger aquifers among the studied 0.1– 41 km 2 scale showed a lagged regime. The results suggest that the selected approach effectively captures the spatially evolving conditions. They also highlight the importance of long-term monitoring for effective decision-making and preparedness for shortages in water availability in the changing climate.

papers.summary: Urban flooding has become one of the most significant challenges for rapidly urbanizing cities, where intensive land development, increasing impervious surfaces, and complex topography substantially amplify surface runoff and flash flood hazards. The aim of this study is to develop an integrated methodological framework for assessing urban flood risk through dynamic hydrological modelling and multi-scenario spatial analysis using Geographic Information Systems. The study was conducted within a highly urbanized micro-catchment located in the Yasamal district of Baku, Azerbaijan, characterized by steep relief, predominantly impermeable clay soils, and dense urban development. The methodology combines Digital Elevation Model analysis, land use and land cover assessment, hydrological soil classification, the Rational and Soil Conservation Service Curve Number methods, runoff concentration modelling based on the National Resources Conservation Service Kinematic Wave approach, and Geographic Information Systems-based spatial analysis. Rainfall scenarios ranging from 1 to 100 mm were simulated to evaluate runoff generation, peak discharge, flood propagation, and the spatial distribution of flood hazards at the individual building level. The results demonstrate that the interaction between relief morphology, intensive urbanization, and low soil infiltration capacity creates favourable conditions for rapid stormwater accumulation and flash flood formation. Approximately 79% of the total runoff is concentrated within three critical topographic depressions, while floodwaters reach the most vulnerable buildings within only 3.0–4.3 minutes under high-intensity rainfall scenarios. Comparative analysis revealed that the Rational method provides more reliable estimates of peak discharge and runoff concentration time, whereas the Soil Conservation Service Curve Number method more accurately predicts runoff volume. Numerical Simulation of the Propagation Characteristics of a Pulse Fracture Network in Shale Reservoirs under Thermo-Hydro-Mechanical-Damage Coupling
papers.summary: Abstract Deep shale reservoirs feature poor physical properties and well-developed dense bedding planes. Conventional hydraulic fracturing produces limited stimulated volume and inadequate activation of natural fractures, failing to effectively boost reservoir permeability, while pulsed fracturing is a promising technique to construct complex fracture networks. The multifield coupled fracture propagation mechanism of pulsed fracturing in high-bedding-density shale remains ambiguous, and the uniformity of fracture stimulation needs optimization. This paper constructs a stress-damage-seepage-temperature four-field coupled model for pulsed fracture propagation, and systematically explores the regulating rules of pulse amplitude, frequency, and confining pressure difference on fracture evolution, considering shale bedding anisotropy. The results reveal three synchronous evolutionary stages of pulsed fracturing: initial compaction, rapid damage accumulation, and stable fracture propagation. Higher pulse amplitudes accelerate fatigue damage and branch fracture growth, and fracture network complexity negatively correlates with pulse frequency, where low-frequency pulses favor continuous seepage channels. Larger confining pressure differences raise fracture propagation resistance and restrain bedding weak plane activation. Increasing pulse amplitude, reducing frequency, and lowering confining pressure difference jointly trigger positive coupling feedback to fully activate bedding planes and form intricate fracture networks. This work offers theoretical guidance for parameter optimization of shale pulsed fracturing.

Microstructure-transport coupling in titaniferous magnetite pre-reduction: Porosity evolution, Ti-phase effects, and modelling for low-carbon ironmaking
papers.summary: Titaniferous magnetite (TTM) is among the largest reserves of underexploited iron ore resources. Titanium-bearing minerals including ilmenite, pseudobrookite, and enriched titanium spinel phases alter reduction mechanisms, pore structure development, and transport phenomena in ways that traditional iron oxide models cannot capture. This review addresses that gap by consolidating recent developments in the solid-state, packed-bed pre-reduction of TTM, a process whose literature remains comparatively scarce relative to conventional hematite, with emphasis on the coupling between microstructural evolution and transport processes across particle, pellet, and reactor scales. Topics covered include porosity transitions from uni-modal to bi-modal pore structures, the competing roles of sintering and pore formation in controlling permeability, the effect of Ti-phase enrichment on the transition from chemical to diffusion control, reaction-front progression, the influence of carbonaceous and gaseous reductants, and multiphysics computational fluid dynamics modelling of heat, gas-phase transport, and phase transformation across scales. Since direct TTM evidence remains sparse relative to conventional ore, this review also develops testable, semi-quantitative hypotheses linking Ti-phase persistence to permeability loss, percolation-threshold shifts, and whisker-versus-dense-shell morphology, alongside three outstanding gaps: the absence of data linking titanium-phase formation to permeability under realistic flowing-gas conditions, the lack of pore-scale investigation under titaniferous conditions, and the absence of a multiphysics CFD model incorporating Fe-Ti-O multicomponent thermochemistry in packed-bed reactors. Insights from synchrotron visualization, thermogravimetric kinetics, and reactor simulation provide a foundation for efficient, low-carbon pre-reduction of titaniferous magnetite.

Distinct Liquefaction Resistance of Fujian Sand Under the Combined Effect of Asymmetric Cyclic Loads and Fabric Anisotropy
papers.summary: Abstract Fabric anisotropy and load asymmetry can both significantly influence the mechanical behavior of sand. To clarify the coupled influence of fabric anisotropy and load asymmetry on liquefaction characteristics, sand specimens with different bedding angles were loaded by cyclic loadings of different degrees of asymmetry under undrained triaxial conditions. The influences of fabric anisotropy on the liquefaction characteristics under different degrees of loading asymmetry were identified through comprehensive analyses of excess pore water pressure generation, axial strain development, and energy dissipation during the cyclic loading. The results indicate that under a symmetric cyclic load, the liquefaction resistance of sand increases with increasing bedding angle. However, when the loading asymmetry increases and exceeds a certain degree, the larger bedding angle leads to lower liquefaction resistance.

papers.title: Unravelling the tectonic and climatic controls on Upper Jurassic mass flow deposits in NE Scotland
papers.summary: The NE Scottish coast between Portgower and Navidale contains an unusual succession of interbedded boulder beds and fine-grained rocks of upper Kimmeridgian to Tithonian (Upper Jurassic) age that have attracted attention for over 150 years. Their juxtaposition next to the Helmsdale Fault has commonly led to the inference that their deposition is entirely fault controlled and shows no systematic ordering. This study presents: the first centimetre-scale reproducible graphic log of this c. 4.3 Ma (610 m) sedimentary succession; new palynomorph biostratigraphy; detailed facies analysis; sketch maps; new ammonite finds and drone footage. The new biostratigraphical data considerably refines four of the seven boundaries. Furthermore, palynology proves the scitulus and hudlestoni zones, and ammonites the elegans zone, in NE Scotland for the first time. Together the data show that the succession is a bimodal system of five fine-grained facies (tiger stripe) and five coarse-grained facies, that it is stratigraphically fairly complete and there are no major faults that remove stratigraphy. Sediment transport was mostly fault parallel. Sequence stratigraphical analysis shows 67 metre-scale cycles interpreted as parasequences and eight depositional sequences that are typically 60-70 metres thick. Parasequences comprise coarsening-upward micro-turbidite packages (composed of tiger stripe facies) usually capped by a pebble-cobble or pebble-boulder debris flow. Sequences comprise a falling stage systems tract of stacked pebble-cobble debris flows or high-density turbidites, a lowstand systems tract where the facies are highly variable laterally and a transgressive systems tract and highstand systems tract, both composed of generally well-developed parasequences. The sequence boundaries are always sharp and some show erosion. papers.title: Time-lapse images for debris flow monitoring at Mount Shasta, California in 2022
papers.summary: Over the summer of 2022 the USGS deployed temporary seismometers, infrasound arrays, and cameras along several drainages at Mount Shasta, California. Twenty-one debris flows were confirmed by the cameras or other observations. This data set consists of images from cameras placed near three drainages (Bolam Creek, Mud Creek, and Whitney Creek). Images were stored on internal Secure Digital (SD) cards and real-time thumbnail images were broadcast via cell modem for real-time monitoring. Time intervals between images were toggled remotely and range from 30 seconds to 10 minutes and images were only collected during daylight hours. The images for each camera are contained in one to three zipped folders (marked as a, b, and c in chronological order), corresponding to SD cards removed from the cameras when full. A separate zipped folder (GIFs) contains daily animations from 0700 PDT and selected debris flows seen at each camera during their operation. Images with identifiable people have been removed.

papers.title: Assessing Geomorphic Effects of Hurricane Hilary, CA 2023
papers.summary: In August 2023, Hurricane Hilary brought widespread heavy rainfall to Southern California. Some normally arid desert areas received more than their typical annual rainfall, which triggered debris flows, flash floods, and large-scale sediment movement. Lidar data was collected shortly after the storm to capture evidence of how the landscape changed during this event. This project and its research is being conducted within the structure of the Center for Land Surface Hazards (CLaSH). Its goal is to document erosion, deposition, impacts on infrastructure, and to improve understanding of cascading hazards. The data also support the development and testing of next-generation hazard models.

papers.title: Volumetric Water Content and Shear Failure of Volcanic Ash: Evidence From Powder Shear Cell Analyses
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Volcanic debris flows are among the most hazardous mass-movement processes because they are unpredictable and can rapidly attain high velocities and destructive power, causing fatalities and damage to buildings and infrastructure. Their initiation and propagation are controlled by a combination of predisposing conditions (topography, catchment morphology, geological/structural setting, etc.) and transient hydrological forcing. Water is often the key agent because it modifies the effective stress state of the soil and can favor excess pore-pressure buildup, thereby directly affecting shear strength. In this study, we investigated how increasing water content modifies the mechanical behavior of three ash-rich soils collected in the Sarno area (Campanian Volcanic Province, Southern Italy). The deposits were tested at volumetric water content values from 0 to 8 percent in 2 percent increments through undrained shear experiments performed with a rheometer under controlled conditions. The results indicate the onset of matric-suction effects associated with water-meniscus formation as the material transitions from dry to moist conditions, accompanied by an initial increase in apparent cohesion and a shift in flow behavior from a free-flowing granular response to a markedly cohesive regime. These results improve the knowledge about the influence of the moisture content on the mechanical stability of volcanic ash soils, providing constraints for predictive modeling and hazard mitigation in volcanic terrains.
